title: Show HN: Jev vs. OpenAI Decision vs. Small Financial World Models: FinBench [video]
author: atul-mehra
body:
Guys - OpenAI Decisions, Jev, World Models are interesting.We ran some tests for the C-suite to decide between OpenAI Decisions vs. their own existing models vs. training their proprietary Financial World Model. Sharing the results of our sample tests.If you like a walkthrough with video of results - see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN1LIF01uHQWe are also trying to reach OpenAI team & community to collaborate on running various tests to help the C-suite to make decisions. 
Which involves which business cases, they wish to map on which Decision models.Summary: Small Financial World Model compared to OpenAI Decisions.This test is not to build a better model. But to help C-suites make informed choices. There are various considerations vizLatency
Cost per decision
On-premises or Hosted APIs
Regulatory & Compliance
Mapping to use cases
Financial modelling or LLM-based reasoning as underlying architecture
We ran tests to:Predict credit defaults
Cross-sell propensity
Churn Risk
Future cash flows
Future state of customers & causal impacts of interventions like no-action, Payment reminders etc.These tests are specific to banking use cases.Why Benchmark & comparison:Small on-prem Decision Models are needed due to latency, cost, regulatory or protecting the proprietary data for Enterprises.This benchmarking helps C-suite executives to decide which option - their in-house models or other options are better. Vaayu FinBench also includes some specific banking-related business cases as examples.World Model also has action-conditioning. Thus, it predicts which decision optimizes the future outcomes. Eg Risk weighted return or prevent default. Core ask from BanksSmall Financial World Model is trained on-premesis on proprietary data for enterprises.Scope - This is only for demonstration purposes to give a glimpse of how to compare various options. The dataset & model size is way too small yet. On a larger proprietary dataset, the results need to be benchmarked.Results:
Latency - A co-located Small Financial World Model way improves latency. Major part may be coming due to network latency. So this is one area where we would like to discuss alternatives with OpenAI team & community. Is there a smaller on-premesis version for Decision Model avaialble for co-location.Credit Defaults - Our Small Financial World model worked worse than Decision API.Cash Churn & Cross Sell propensity - Our Small Financial World model improved marginally. It’s obvious that since Decision API hasnt seen the propreitary data. The marginal improvement shows model is learning..but our model is very very small (Few 100 thousand parameters) trained on small dataset.. But test demonstrates - architecture is capable of learning better.Action conditions outcomes - This is available in World Model …but we aren’t aware of this in Decision API yet.Financial Modelling - Model is trained finance native can handle temporal & causal scenariosIf you like a walkthrough - see this video - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UN1LIF01uHQDisclaimer: This is quick tests results & has some know issues. This is only for demonstration purpose. We have included OpenAI Decisions for now...Including Jev in next releases. At the moment talking to C-suite & Banks for what they wish.We find Decision API & World Models interesting developments especially in finance & enterprises space. Looking forward to collaborate with OpenAI team & community how to enable C-suite to make choices…which are underway right now at enterprises.

title: Show HN: Checkered Chat – QR codes with decoy messages and Shamir splits
author: HoneyWired
body:
Checkered Chat 
What it is 
 How 
 Modes 
 Everywhere 
 Print 
 Pricing 
 Privacy 
 Support 
Download 
iPhone · Apple Watch · iMessage
Chat with QR codes.
Turn your words into a code. Hold up your screen, print it on
 a sticker, or drop it into Messages. Any camera reads the public note;
 Checkered Chat reads the one underneath — or asks the question only
 they can answer. No accounts, no cloud, and neither of you has to be
 online.
No inbox · No server · One unlock
Pause the video 
Three steps. Not one of them asks for an email address.
Write it. A message, a mode, and you’re done composing.
 The meter beside it tells you whether the code will survive at the size
 you’re printing.
Hand it over. Hold up your screen, save the picture, print a sheet
 of stickers, or send it in Messages. The code is the message, so however
 it travels is however it travels.
They scan it. An open code opens in any camera. Everything else
 opens in Checkered Chat, which asks the question, lifts the cover, or
 gathers the pieces. In Messages it’s just a tap — no camera at
 all, for anyone who has the app.
So what do you actually make with one?
Fair question. “QR code messenger” doesn’t answer it.
Scavenger hunts
Print a sheet of stickers, a clue in each one, and hide them around a park or an office. Put a riddle on the last code so nobody can skip to the end.
Cards worth opening twice
Two notes in one code. The table scans “Happy birthday” off their own phones; the person it’s for gets the longer version.
Group gifts
Split the note across five codes and pick the arithmetic — any three open it, any two open nothing. Everyone has to turn up.
Notes in a lunchbox
Or a jacket pocket, or taped inside a book. It’s a picture, so it goes wherever paper goes.
Escape rooms and pop-ups
A code on a table tent that isn’t a link, can’t redirect anybody, and works with the wifi down.
The long one, across a room
Too much text for a single code becomes a set of frames the other phone catches in any order. No pairing, no network, nothing to join.
A code from here carries text, and only text.
Nothing in one is a link, so one handed to you by a stranger has nowhere to
 take you — which isn’t true of QR codes in general, and is the reason
 this is worth saying.
Never a web address, never anything your phone could be talked into opening.
 That’s a rule the app is built on rather than a setting you can turn off.
Five ways to say it. One way to show it.
Open and Locked are free. Decoy, Split and Animated are the unlock, and your
 first three are on the house.
Open
Ordinary text in an ordinary code. Anyone’s camera reads it, which is sometimes exactly what you want.
Locked
A question only they can answer. “What did we have for breakfast?” — capitals and punctuation don’t matter, because nobody remembers their own punctuation.
Decoy
Two notes in one code. Any other camera reads the first; Checkered Chat reads both. It’s the birthday card that scans as “Happy birthday” for the whole table and as something better for the person it’s for.
Split
One message across several codes, and you choose the arithmetic: any three of five open it, any two tell you nothing at all. Not less — nothing.
Animated
A message too long for one code, played as a set of frames the other phone catches in any order, with a ring that fills as they arrive.
Show mode
Full screen, full brightness, and a timer: show a code for five seconds and it clears itself. Turn the phone over and it’s gone.
What it looks like.
Every one of these is the app itself, captured on a phone.
Writing. The meter says whether it will survive printing. 
Showing. Full screen, and it can clear itself after a few seconds. 
A decoy: the first note above, the longer one below. 
What Checkered Chat shows: both notes, in the order they were written. 
A question lock. The question travels in the clear. 
Answering. Capitals and punctuation don’t matter. 
One piece of a split message, ready to hand over. 
Collecting a split set. The ring fills as pieces arrive. 
A sheet of labels, measured from the manufacturer’s template. 
Shapes, color, and the size it’s going to be read at. 
Pause the video 
Writing a decoy in the drawer, sending it, and the
 other side opening it. The codes are real — point a camera at the
 screen and you get the cover story, the same as anyone else in the chat
 would. 
Right where you’re already talking.
In Messages. Write a code in the app drawer and it goes straight into the
 conversation — no screenshotting, no second device. Anyone who has
 Checkered Chat taps the bubble and the message opens; no camera is involved at
 all. Everyone else sees a code they can point a camera at. Put a decoy in a
 group chat and the whole table reads the first note off their own cameras, which
 is the fun of it at a party.
A long message goes in as a set of frames, and the bubble plays them. That
 isn’t a picture Messages is showing you — the app draws it in the
 conversation itself. That’s why a tap opens the message rather than a video
 player.
On your wrist. Send a code from your phone to the Watch and it draws it
 there, at the largest size the screen allows — a decoy, or a long message
 as a set of frames the Watch plays in turn. The Watch tells you when one
 arrives, and says only that one has: never the message, never a preview, not
 even a decoy’s first note. A lock screen is the most public thing you own.
Write a short one on the wrist with dictation or Scribble, in whichever way
 round your phone is set — choose white on black there and the wrist
 follows. Pin the ones you use often and a complication opens straight into
 them.
The Watch shows codes; it never reads them. There’s no camera on a Watch, so
 the wrist is always the thing being read.
In Messages
Two notes, one code. Everyone in the chat reads the first one. 
It lands as an ordinary code. Any camera can read it — and gets
 the first note. 
The app shows both. The cover story on top, the real note
 underneath. 
Or lock it with a question only they can answer. 
It lands as a locked code. You need the answer to open it. 
It asks the question first. The question travels with the code —
 the answer never does. 
Tap it and it opens. No camera, no second phone, no scanning. 
Send it as a plain picture instead, and nobody gets the tap — the
 app tells you which you’re choosing. 
On your wrist
What the phone sent, and the ones you pinned. 
Full screen, as large as the glass allows, ready for somebody else’s
 camera. 
Write a short one there with dictation or Scribble. 
Stickers that actually scan.
Codes are drawn as paths and exported as vector PDFs, so a two-inch sticker is
 two inches on paper — not two inches minus whatever the renderer rounded
 away. Every sheet in the catalog is measured from the manufacturer’s own
 published template rather than typed in from memory, and the app says which
 product each one came from. Sizes it hasn’t measured aren’t in the list: for
 anything else, including A4 stock, you enter the measurements once and
 they’re kept.
Printers drift, so there’s an alignment sheet: print the outlines, hold them
 against a real sheet of labels, and nudge in half-millimeter steps. The nudge is
 kept for that stock, so it’s found once.
Print at 100%. Everything else on this page is a preference; that one is
 arithmetic.
One fair price. Read everything for free.
$9.99 unlock paid once — no subscription, no ads, nothing collected 
Reading and scanning any code, including a decoy somebody hands you 
 Free, always 
Writing open and locked codes, and showing them full screen 
 Free 
Decoys, split sets, animated sets, module shapes and frames, sticker sheets 
 $9.99 once 
Subscription, ads, anything collected about you 
 None of it 
Your first three codes in a paid mode are on the house — three in total,
 spend them how you like.
There’s no server to validate a receipt against, so the App Store is asked
 directly what your Apple Account owns. Restore purchases lives in About.
Privacy Policy
Last updated September 29, 2026
Checkered Chat collects nothing, sends nothing, and stores nothing about you. This is not a promise about careful handling. There is no data, and there is no networking code in the app to send it with.
What leaves your device
Nothing. There are no analytics, no crash reporting, no advertising identifiers, no accounts and no server. Turn on airplane mode and the app behaves identically, because it never had anything to say to the network in the first place.
The only outward links are the ones in About — this page, support and terms — which open in your browser when you tap them. Tapping one leaves the app; nothing about you goes with it.
The camera
Checkered Chat asks for camera access because scanning a code is half the app. Frames are examined on the device, looking only for QR codes. Nothing is recorded, photographed, saved or transmitted. 
Your photos
Importing a picture of a code uses the system picker, which hands the app the one picture you chose and nothing else — the app has no access to your library and never asks for it.
Saving a code to your photos asks for add-only permission the first time, which lets the app put a picture in and gives it no ability to read anything already there.
On your watch
If you send a code to an Apple Watch, the watch can tell you it arrived. That notification says “A code arrived” and nothing else — never the message, never a preview, not even the first note of a decoy. A lock screen is the most public surface you own, and a message you had to make a code for does not belong on it. Reading it still means opening the app.
What is written to disk
Only settings, never messages. Whether you have seen the introduction. The printer alignment nudges you save on the sticker sheet screen, kept per sheet of stock so you do not have to find them twice. Whether you have bought the unlock, and how many of the three free codes you have used. And the mode and options you last chose in the Messages app, so it opens where you left it.
The look you last chose, too: module shape, the two colors, whether there is a center mark, how fast an animated set plays, and the size you are printing at. A house color you use every day should not have to be picked every day. What you wrote is not among them — not the message, not either half of a decoy, not a lock’s question. The app remembers that you like round modules in navy. It does not remember a word you put in one.
The last three are shared between the app and its Messages extension, because they are two separate programs that have to agree — otherwise the three free codes would be three in each, and buying the unlock in one would not unlock the other. Nothing you write or scan is among them. The Messages extension remembers that you last chose Decoy; it does not remember a single word of what you wrote.
Messages are never written down. What you write exists while you are writing it. What you scan exists while you are reading it, and is gone when you close it — there is no history, no inbox and no way to ask the app what it saw yesterday, because it did not keep it.
Your purchase is recorded by the App Store, as every purchase is. The app asks Apple what you own; it does not keep a record of its own and has no receipt server to check with.
Children
Checkered Chat collects no personal information from anyone, of any age. There is no mechanism by which it could, so there is nothing collected from a child either — no accounts, no sign-up, no directory, and no way for a stranger to reach anyone through the app. A code arrives because somebody handed it over.
The App Store listing is rated 4+, which is what Apple's age questionnaire produces for it: there is no objectionable content in the app, and nothing in it but what its user wrote.
Changes
If any of this ever stops being true, this page changes first and the app's version notes will say so plainly. The date at the top is when this page last changed.
Who to ask
Checkered Chat is made by HoneyWired LLC in Chicago, Illinois. Questions about this policy, or about anything above, go to support@honeywired.com . There is no data of yours for us to show you, correct or delete — that is the whole of this page — but the address is a real one and it is read.
Terms & EULA
Last updated September 29, 2026
1. License
Checkered Chat is licensed, not sold, under Apple's standard Licensed Application End User License Agreement, for use across the devices connected to your Apple Account. The paid features are a one-time purchase with no recurring charges and no subscription.
That agreement is the license. What follows supplements it with the things particular to this app, and where the two ever disagree, Apple's governs.
2. Age
The App Store listing is rated 4+, which is what the age questionnaire produces for this app: there is nothing in it unsuitable for a younger reader — no accounts, no strangers, no content but your own. The rating describes the app's contents and is not a recommendation about who should use it. A message only one person can read is a fine thing between friends and a poor thing to hand around a school; section 7 asks you not to use it that way, and that request is the part that matters.
3. Not a security product
Checkered Chat is a toy. It is not encrypted messaging, not a password manager, and not a means of protecting sensitive information. A locked code can be guessed at indefinitely by whoever holds it. A decoy hides a message from a casual glance, not from anyone who examines what the code actually contains. Do not use any of it for something whose disclosure would matter.
4. Cryptography
Locked codes are closed using cryptography built into Apple's own operating systems — AES-GCM and PBKDF2, reached through Apple's CryptoKit and CommonCrypto frameworks. Checkered Chat writes none of its own, with one exception: the arithmetic that splits a key across several codes, which is Shamir's Secret Sharing — a scheme published in 1979 and implemented here from the published description, not invented for this app. None of this makes the app a security product; section 3 above is the plain truth and this section does not soften it.
Some countries restrict the import, use or export of software that performs cryptography. The app does not know or ask where you are. Using it in accordance with the law where you are is your responsibility.
5. Nothing is recoverable
The app keeps no copy of anything you write or scan. If you lose a code, the message in it is gone, and we cannot retrieve it — not as a policy, but because it was never anywhere but in your hands.
6. Screenshots and photographs
A code on a screen can be photographed, and a printed code can be picked up. The app tells you when a screenshot is taken while a code is showing; it cannot prevent one, and does not claim to.
7. Acceptable use
Checkered Chat is for notes between people who want to exchange them. Do not use it to harass, intimidate, frighten or follow anyone. Do not send codes to someone who has asked you to stop, and do not leave them where they are likely to be found by a person who would rather not have found them. Do not use it to break the law, or to carry anything it is illegal to hold or to pass on.
One thing deserves saying on its own, because it is the only misuse this app makes easier than it would otherwise be. A decoy exists so a message looks dull to everyone except its reader. It is not there to trick somebody into scanning something they would not have scanned, and it is not there to carry content past a person or a process whose job is to look at it. That is not what a decoy is for.
There is no report button, and the reason is worth saying plainly rather than hiding. Nothing you write reaches us: no server, no account, no copy. So there is nobody here who could read a reported code, and a button leading nowhere would be worse than no button. If somebody is using a code against you, the code itself is the evidence — keep it. Take it to whoever carried it: the platform the message arrived on, your school or workplace, or the police. A code inserted in Messages sits in a conversation Apple’s own reporting already covers.
What you write, who you hand it to, and where you leave it are yours.
8. Printing
Label measurements are taken from manufacturers' published templates and are provided as a convenience. Printers vary; check an alignment sheet before committing a sheet of stock, and print at 100%.

Support
Questions, bugs, a scanner that will not read a printed code, or an idea worth building — write to support@honeywired.com .
Two things help enormously: what the code was made in (Open, Locked, Decoy, Split or Animated), and whether it was on a screen or on paper. Printed problems are usually size problems, and the app will tell you which size would have worked.
Questions we expect
Do other people need the app to read my code? 
 Not for an Open code — any camera reads it, because it is ordinary text in an ordinary QR code. Locked, Decoy, Split and Animated codes need Checkered Chat, because there is something to unlock, uncover or reassemble.
What is free and what costs? 
 Reading is always free. Scanning any code costs nothing, including a decoy somebody hands you, and so does writing an open or locked message and showing it on your screen.
Making decoys, split sets and animated sets, and printing sticker sheets, are the one-time unlock. Your first three codes in a paid mode are free — three in total, spent on whichever modes you like — so you can see what one is like before deciding.
Can a code somebody hands me do something to my phone? 
 Not one of ours. A Checkered Chat code carries text and nothing else — never a web address, never anything your phone could be talked into opening. That is a rule the app is built on rather than a setting you can turn off, and it is why a code from a stranger is safe to point a camera at.
This is worth knowing because it is not true of QR codes in general. Most codes on posters and menus are links, and a link can go anywhere. Ours are not links, so there is nowhere for one to take you.
How safe is a locked code?

I paid, and a feature is locked again. 
 Open About and tap Restore purchases. That asks the App Store what your Apple Account owns. If it still says nothing, check that you are signed in with the account you bought it on.
Can I get a refund? 
 Yes, but not from us — Apple handles every App Store purchase and refund, and we never see the transaction. Go to reportaproblem.apple.com , sign in, and pick the purchase. If something about the app is the reason, we would like to hear it either way.
What age is this for? 
 The listing is rated 4+, which is what the App Store's age questionnaire produces for it: there is nothing objectionable in the app, no accounts, no strangers and no content but your own. That is a statement about what is inside it, not a recommendation. A message only one person can read is a fine thing between friends and a poor thing to hand around a school, so: please do not use it to make somebody's life harder. title: Show HN: Infinity – Git-style branching for AI chats
author: nkotov
body: Hello HN, I'm Nik. I built Infinity for myself because I tend to love to rabbit-hole on various subjects.I usually have 3-4 windows open for ChatGPT desktop + Claude + Ollama. Typically, I'd ask a question, see something interesting in the answer, and then keep expanding on it. The mental chain of thought eventually gets lost and I would start from scratch again. Second, I also wanted to compare answers across multiple models. From there, pick and use the best one and continue.So I built Infinity for myself. Multiple windows, multiple chats. Projects all aligned in one place. But the best part is when you start highlighting any part of the response - you can branch off and fork into new chat sessions from there without losing your original chain of thought.It's a native Mac app written in Swift. You can use all the popular cloud models that you already pay for but on top of that, you can use local models as well. You can even set out what each model's job is and assign certain models for certain jobs.It's free, there's no account, no analytics on the actual app. Everything is stored locally. Just download, connect up, and get going.Still extremely early but if there is interest, would love to hear what works and what doesn't!

title: Show HN: NASA's Swift telescope's 22 years in orbit, rebuilt from its archive
author: mrroryflint
body:
SWIFT: A Life in Orbit

3D view unavailable because WebGL is off or not supported. The map shows the same ground track. The pale dot is where the Sun is overhead.

# SWIFT

A life in orbit.

2004– 2026

For nearly 22 years, it circled Earth to watch the universe. Follow its orbit and see what it observed.

Start exploring

Built from the public archive of NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, held by HEASARC, the Swift Data Center and the UK Swift Science Data Centre.

SWIFT A life in orbit

23 April 2009

07:38:28 UTC

Mission
: day 1,615
Below Swift
: 20.65° S 163.33° E
Altitude
: 602 km
Speed
: 7.55 km/s

Reconstructed position · elements 6.8 h from epoch · ±0.9 km

### No exposure recorded

The instrument logs have nothing at this time. Usually Swift was turning, passing through the South Atlantic Anomaly, or paused.

Observation Close observation

Swift was unknown pointed at unknown

Target
Instruments
: none recorded
Pointing
: not recorded

Original data

## Moments

Key events from the mission, each with sources. Choosing one takes you to that moment, and to the observation if there is one.

Early days, 2004–2005

20 November 2004 · 17:16 UTC

#### Launch

Swift launched on a Boeing Delta II from Cape Canaveral at 12:16 p.m. EST. It separated from the rocket about 80 minutes later.

11 December 2004 · 00:45 UTC Observation

#### First X-ray image

The X-ray Telescope's first target was Cassiopeia A, the remains of a supernova.

17 December 2004 · 07:28 UTC Observation

#### First gamma-ray burst

GRB 041217 was the first burst Swift located on board. It could not yet turn to bursts automatically.

27 December 2004

#### Magnetar flare

A month after launch Swift recorded a giant flare from the magnetar SGR 1806-20, about 50,000 light-years away. NASA said it released more energy than the Sun gives out in 150,000 years.

5 April 2005

#### Science begins

After four and a half months of checks, normal science operations started.

9 May 2005 · 04:00 UTC Observation

#### A short burst pinned down

GRB 050509B lasted a fraction of a second. It was the first short burst located quickly and accurately, near an elliptical galaxy at a probable redshift of 0.225. This pointed to two merging compact stars.

4 July 2005 · 07:02 UTC Observation

#### Deep Impact

Swift observed comet 9P/Tempel 1 on the day NASA's Deep Impact probe hit it.

4 September 2005 · 01:51 UTC Observation

#### Distance record

GRB 050904, at redshift 6.29, beat the previous gamma-ray burst record of 4.5.

18 February 2006 · 03:34 UTC Observation

#### A star exploding

GRB 060218 lasted about 2,100 seconds. Its X-rays were read as the shock wave breaking out of a Wolf-Rayet star, which then became the supernova SN 2006aj.

9 January 2008 · 13:32 UTC Observation

#### Supernova caught as it began

While observing another supernova in NGC 2770, 90 million light-years away, the X-ray Telescope recorded a five-minute X-ray flash. It was SN 2008D, seen at the moment it exploded.

19 March 2008 · 06:12 UTC Observation

#### Visible to the naked eye

The optical flash from GRB 080319B reached magnitude 5.3, bright enough to see without a telescope, from 7.5 billion light-years away.

23 April 2009 · 07:55 UTC Observation

#### Most distant explosion

GRB 090423 had a redshift of about 8.2. Its light left when the universe was about 630 million years old.

13 April 2010

#### 500th burst

GRB 100413B was Swift's 500th gamma-ray burst.

28 March 2011 · 12:57 UTC Observation

#### Star torn apart

Swift J1644+57 was a Sun-like star pulled apart by a black hole 3.9 billion light-years away. A jet from the event pointed straight at Earth.

27 April 2013 · 07:47 UTC Observation

#### Record-bright burst

GRB 130427A arrived while Swift was turning between targets. The BAT picked it up less than a minute after Fermi. Its gamma-ray fluence was the highest recorded up to then.

27 October 2015 Observation

#### 1,000th burst

GRB 151027B was Swift's 1,000th gamma-ray burst.

17 August 2017 · 12:41 UTC Observation

#### Neutron star merger

About 15 hours after gravitational waves from merging neutron stars reached Earth, Swift found a fading ultraviolet source in NGC 4993. It was the first ultraviolet light seen from a kilonova.

9 October 2022 · 13:16 UTC Observation

#### Brightest burst on record

Fermi saw GRB 221009A first. Swift's BAT triggered at 14:10 UTC and at first logged it as a new source in our galaxy. It turned out to be the brightest gamma-ray burst ever recorded.

11 August 2007

#### Gyroscope failure

A gyroscope failed on 11 August 2007. Operations were back to normal on 19 October.

6 February 2017

#### Neil Gehrels

Neil Gehrels, Swift's principal investigator since the start, died on 6 February 2017.

10 January 2018

#### Renamed

The Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer was renamed the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory.

18 January 2022

#### Reaction wheel problem

A reaction wheel fault put Swift in safe mode from 18 January to 17 February 2022.

15 March 2024

#### Two-gyro mode

A noisy gyroscope sent Swift into safe mode on 15 March 2024. A software update let it point using two gyros, and science resumed on 3 April with better pointing than before.

24 September 2025

#### Plan to raise the orbit

Swift's orbit was dropping faster because of high solar activity. NASA gave Katalyst Space Technologies a contract to try to boost it.

17 December 2025

#### Pointing to reduce drag

From December 2025 Swift replaced many targets with pointings that reduced drag. The catalogue lists 57,769 of these 'DragPoint' observations between 17 December 2025 and 26 August 2026.

11 February 2026

#### Science paused

Swift paused most science operations to get ready for the boost.

3 July 2026 · 08:36 UTC

#### LINK launches

Katalyst's LINK spacecraft launched on a Pegasus XL rocket from Kwajalein to meet Swift.

19 August 2026

#### Boost called off

LINK had problems with its reaction wheels and thrusters. NASA announced it would not capture or boost Swift. LINK had come within 12 to 15 km.

26 August 2026

#### Science restarts

Swift restarted observations with its X-ray and UV/optical telescopes. Automatic turning to new bursts came back on 21 September.

20 October 2026 · 18:49 UTC Observation

#### Final observation

On 20 October, at about 275 km, Swift could no longer keep up with the drag. Its last catalogued observation started at 18:49 UTC.

4 November 2026 · 12:39 UTC

#### Re-entry

The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift re-entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra, Indonesia, at about 3.4° N, 98.6° E. Most of it was expected to burn up.

## The archive

458,237 observations of 126,070 targets: the full Swift Master Catalog, downloaded 2026-11-06. 0 have images processed for this site, and the rest show the archive's own quick-look images.

## About the data

Everything here comes from public records. This page explains where, how it was worked out, and how accurate it is.

### What this is

NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory (NORAD 28485, COSPAR 2004-047A) launched on 20 November 2004 and re-entered the atmosphere over North Sumatra on 4 November 2026. This site works out where it was at any moment, what it was pointed at, and for some observations shows the images and measurements it recorded.

### How reliable is the position?

Reconstructed. Calculated from the mission's own orbital elements, using the set closest in time (within 3 days). Older data. The closest set is 3 to 10 days away. This is rare; the longest gap is 20.7 days, in June 2007. Extrapolated. After the last set of elements (20 October 2026). Shown for 36 hours at most. Unavailable. No position is shown. The mission archive has no elements from 21 October until re-entry.

For processed observations, positions come from that observation's own orbit file and pointing from its attitude file. Otherwise the pointing is the catalogue's pointing during a logged exposure. While Swift was turning, the direction is estimated between targets and drawn fainter. The clouds are a NASA composite, not the weather on the day shown.

### Checks

Things we found along the way. The catalogue's start and stop times leave out the spacecraft clock drift. By 2026 they are about 34 seconds late, which would put Swift about 260 km out of place, so every time here is corrected using the mission's clock calibration file. The mission's orbit files also skip precession when they give longitude (about 0.36° off by 2026), so this site works longitude out separately. Older orbit files were timed with the uncorrected clock, and are adjusted for that.

HEASARC Swift Master Catalog · XRT and UVOT logs · Burst Advocate GRB list · Swift Data Center archive · Swift clock calibration (CALDB) · CCMC Swift re-entry challenge · UK Swift Science Data Centre light curves (Evans et al. 2007, 2009) · Yale Bright Star Catalogue (HEASARC bsc5p).

Images: Blue Marble Next Generation, July 2004 (NASA Earth Observatory, Reto Stöckli). Black Marble 2016 (NASA Earth Observatory, Joshua Stevens; Suomi NPP VIIRS data, Miguel Román, NASA GSFC). Blue Marble clouds (NASA Earth Observatory). GEBCO relief and bathymetry (NASA Earth Observatory, Jesse Allen; GEBCO/BODC). Deep Star Maps 2020 (NASA Goddard Scientific Visualization Studio; Gaia DR2: ESA/Gaia/DPAC). Swift 3D model (NASA/Christopher R. Meaney). The spacecraft is drawn much larger than its real 5.6 m so you can see it. NASA material is used under NASA's media guidelines. This site is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

Mission dates and facts were checked against NASA, GCN Circulars and published papers. Each moment lists its sources.

Before you download.
What is Monetor?
 Monetor is an iPhone finance app for automatic expense tracking without a bank connection. Free includes eligible Apple Pay Shortcuts, supported payment-notification tracking, manual entry, budgets, savings goals and multiple currencies. Pro adds premium AI insights, advanced reports and financial tools.
Do I need to connect my bank?
 No. Monetor does not connect to your bank account or use Plaid. You choose supported Shortcuts automations, scan receipts or enter transactions manually. Setup, device compatibility and service availability apply to automatic tracking.
How does automatic tracking work?
 Automatic tracking is included in Free. Set up a Wallet Transaction automation and the Monetor Shortcut on a compatible iPhone with iOS 17+. Payment-notification tracking requires iOS 27+, supported source apps, setup, permissions, consent and service availability. These methods capture eligible new events, not past Wallet or notification history. Manual entry fills the gaps and works on iOS 15.1+.
What does Free include, and what does Pro add?
 Free includes automatic tracking where supported, manual entry, categories, search, two total wallets including the default wallet, multi-currency support, one successful receipt scan per account, week/month analytics, budgets, savings goals, subscriptions and manual loans with reminders. Pro adds more wallets, receipt scanning without the Free quota, premium AI insights, advanced reports and yearly comparisons, subscription overlap insights, loan document/refund tools and CSV, PDF and XLSX exports. Fair-use service limits apply.
Does the Free receipt scan allowance reset each month?
 No. Free includes one successful receipt scan per account, not one per month. A usable extraction consumes the allowance even if you do not save the transaction. Failed or unreadable scans do not consume it. Pro removes this Free quota, subject to fair-use service limits.
Can I track loans without Pro?
 Yes. Manual loan tracking, payments and reminders are included in Free. Pro adds loan document import and premium loan/refund tools. Existing imported loan schedules remain accessible after returning to Free; there is no separate Free loan trial.
How much does Monetor cost? Is there a trial?
 Monetor is free to download, and automatic tracking is included in Free where supported. See your local price and available offers in the App Store. Monthly and yearly subscriptions renew automatically unless canceled; Lifetime is a one-time purchase. The purchase sheet confirms current plans, prices and terms. Any trial depends on the offer and your eligibility.
Is my data private?
 Monetor never asks for bank credentials and does not sell your data. Account data is encrypted at rest. Optional AI insights, receipt scanning and payment-notification tracking send the text or images they need to the processors named in the privacy policy, with your consent.
Do I need Pro for budgets or savings goals?
 No. Budgets and savings goals are included in Free. There is no one-goal restriction. Pro adds deeper analysis and premium financial tools.
Is Monetor available on Android or the web?
 Monetor is currently an iPhone app, available on the App Store. It requires iOS 15.1 or later for manual tracking, with newer iOS versions and additional setup for automatic tracking.

Built for Production Excellence

Static & Media

 Native Rust file streaming with kernel sendfile and HTTP 304 caching. Includes zero-setup dynamic finders fallback for development and automated collectstatic workflows. 
Edge Shield

 Instantly drops automated scanners (probing for .php , /.env , /wp-admin/ ) at the gateway in <0.35 microseconds. Shields Django middleware, sessions, and database connection pools. 
DoS Defense

Observability
 Deep Health & Prometheus
 Built-in /alive , /ready , /startup , and /metrics endpoints. Compatible out-of-the-box with AWS ALBs, Docker healthchecks, Prometheus, and Kubernetes probes. 
Zero Config
 WSGI & ASGI Auto-Detection
 Run any project with python manage.py serve . Seamlessly auto-detects WSGI_APPLICATION or ASGI_APPLICATION from your settings with zero extra config files. 
The Django-Native Advantage 
 Django was developed with a batteries-included philosophy and gracefully handles complex web application challenges. But in production—whether running on a single Docker container, an AWS/Fly.io PaaS, or an autoscaling Kubernetes cluster—Django needs more than generic server wrappers like Gunicorn. 
 It's Not Just About Running a Container 
 Generic servers like Gunicorn, Uvicorn, and Nginx know nothing about Django settings, URL patterns, or database lifecycles. Hurricane brings Django-native intelligence to the application server layer: 
 Zero-Nginx Architecture: Serve static and media files natively with kernel sendfile speed, or develop with live dynamic finders without running collectstatic . 
 Edge Attack Immunity: Automated bot vulnerability scans ( wp-login.php , .env ) are dropped at Tier 2 without ever touching Django middlewares or database connections. 
 Migration & Health Synchronization: Preflight database migrations ( --check-migrations-apply ) prevent traffic routing until the database is ready. 
 Traffic Shedding & Deadlock Detection: Real queue depth metrics signal load balancers and orchestrators when worker queues saturate, diverting traffic before requests time out. 
 Hurricane solves these architectural friction points directly at the server layer, giving your Django applications the reliability and resilience required in modern cloud platforms. 
 Proven Track Record 
 Developed and maintained by Blueshoe and open-source contributors: 
 Battle-tested in Production: Running critical Django workloads across enterprise Kubernetes clusters since 2020. 
 Thorough Test Coverage: Comprehensive test suite with automated Kubernetes end-to-end (k3d) validation and cross-process telemetry tests. 
 Independently Benchmarked: 2x throughput increase and 100% elimination of false probe flaps verified in the django-hurricane-bench suite. 
 Cloud-Native Standards: Fully compliant with CNCF standards, OpenMetrics, and 12-factor application guidelines.

title: Show HN: Botel – always reachable agents you pay for only while they're working
author: 4ver
body: I built a pay-as-you-go two star hotel for bots that you’re only charged for while it’s active. Typically wakes in under a second, runs on a vm, and costs very little while it’s paused.In my free time I’ve been building a firecracker based vm orchestration platform. In order to dogfood the thing I put together a place to run agent harnesses (openclaw etc) on machines but only pay for them when they are in use. What started as a demo has grown legs into a more unique product than the platform.Botel has prebaked templates for each harness, with a daemon of mine running beside it monitoring the harness’ activity. It communicates out to the host over a link-local self api; instructing when to pause or wake next based on stored schedules. With a proxy in front to wake on http. The harnesses are preconfigured to point to my llm gateway that proxies through to openrouter.One of the biggest struggles while building it was preventing claude from going off the rails with hotel metaphors in the ui. Once it sees a joke it really strangles the hell out of it.A more real ;) awkward part is that the harnesses don’t expose exactly what I needed in order to detect activity. I'm still struggling with how to handle the fact that background job can be short or long lived (http/dev servers etc). I’m hoping to propose changes to hermes, openclaw, and dsh soon for a consistent way to know what kind of a job is running with annotated lifecycle hooks.Some of the nicest things about the bot hotel are:- You get a proper linux vm with sudo, so you can ssh in, scp, or run docker.- You can ask the agent to expose something publicly or privately (behind your login). A port gets a unique hostname/url. Those endpoints also wake the vm. So you could build and host a little app or self host something.- Guided telegram setup. It’s pretty awkward in general/my setup hopefully takes some of the edge off.A friend of mine who built a website for his local orienteering club has used this to make it easy for peoge on the committee to update news and events. All in all it should cost something like 40 cents a month to run so long as the club members don’t get too friendly with the agent.If you’re interested, give the thing a spin. The first 50 signups get $2 credit. Price is pretty low at 3c per GB of ram per hour awake, plus a few cents per GB-month asleep. You use credit for inference or byok.Let me know how you get on and whether you have any ideas or requests for it. Thx!

| `DrawDock- -windows-x64-setup.exe` | Recommended per-user Windows installation |
| `DrawDock- -windows-x64-portable.zip` | Extract and run `drawdock-launcher.exe`; keep the bundled files together |
| `DrawDock- -android.apk` | Android tablet client, signed with the project's release key |

Windows packages include **ADB and FFmpeg**; a separate Android SDK is not
required for normal packaged-host use. Verify downloads against `SHA256SUMS.txt`.
The matching third-party source archive is included with each release.

> [!CAUTION]
> Windows binaries are currently **not Authenticode-signed**. Their publisher
> metadata is **Mike Cerreto**, not a verified signing identity. Do not bypass
> operating-system security warnings. See release and signing details.

Already have both apps? Go directly to first connection.

 

## 🚀 Installation and first connection

**Start with USB:** install → connect → start the host → pair → draw.

**Have ready:** a Windows 11 x64 PC, an Android 11+ tablet with a compatible
active pen, and a **USB data cable** (not a charging-only cable).
See compatibility for
hardware and OS boundaries.

### 1. Install on both devices

Download the Windows installer and Android APK from the **same
release**.

| Where | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Windows PC** | Run `DrawDock- -windows-x64-setup.exe`, then open **DrawDock** |
| **Android tablet** | Open `DrawDock- -android.apk` on the tablet, follow Android's installation prompts, then open **DrawDock** |

**Ready to continue:** DrawDock is open on both devices.
The Windows installer is per-user; it does not install USB drivers, change
firewall rules or request elevation. The unsigned-Windows warning above still
applies.

Building from source instead? Follow Development and
Android installation.

### 2. Connect and authorize USB

1. **On the tablet:** enable **USB debugging** in Android's **Developer options**.
 The steps to reveal Developer options vary by manufacturer.
2. **Connect the tablet to the PC** with the USB data cable.
3. **On the tablet:** accept the USB debugging authorization prompt only if it
 identifies the PC you intend to use.

**Ready to continue:** in the Windows host, click **Refresh** and find your
authorized tablet in the **USB device** dropdown.
If it is missing or unauthorized, start with USB troubleshooting;
some tablets need an OEM Windows USB driver.

### 3. Start the Windows host

In the **Windows DrawDock window**:

1. Set **Monitor** to the PC screen or projector you want to annotate.
2. Set **Video encoder** to **Software (x264)** or to **NVIDIA NVENC** if you have NVIDA GPU for the first connection.
3. Select your authorized tablet under **USB device**.
4. Select the **USB / ADB** listener row, then click **Enable selected**.
 Leave the private LAN listener off for this first USB test.

**Ready to continue:** the USB listener is marked **[ON]**.

### 4. Pair the tablet with this PC

| Order | Where | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Windows PC** | Keep the enabled USB listener selected and click **Pair tablet / QR** |
| 2 | **Android tablet** | In DrawDock, choose **Connect > Scan QR**, allow camera access if desired, scan the PC's invitation and confirm the endpoint |
| 3 | **Windows PC** | Approve the tablet in the native pairing dialog |

No camera? Use the Android app's manual invitation entry instead.
See pairing instructions.

**Ready to continue:** the host reports a connected tablet and the selected
Windows display appears in the tablet workspace. Wait until the video is ready.

### 5. Try your first annotation

Open a browser, document or presentation on the **selected Windows display**.
On the tablet, choose **Pen tools > Pen** and draw inside the mirrored image.
Use **Pen tools** to try shapes, colors or the laser pointer.

> [!TIP]
> **Success means the same marks appear on both the tablet and the physical PC
> monitor/projector.** Marks visible only on the tablet are not a successful
> end-to-end test.

Completed objects and Blackboard/Grid settings are saved privately on the
tablet before transmission. If USB or Wi-Fi drops, the saved drawing stays
visible with editing paused; DrawDock retries the same authenticated endpoint
and restores it to its original monitor. Backgrounding pauses retries until
you return. **Disconnect / Stop retrying** retains the drawing and stops retries;
after restarting the app, tap **Connect** to recover it.

| After the first test | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Connect again** | With the same Windows USB listener enabled, tap **Connect** on the tablet; a remembered device does not need another QR scan or approval |
| **Finish** | Choose **Stop all** to stop listeners, or **Quit** to exit the Windows host. Closing its window with **X** only hides it to the tray |

 
 Prefer Wi-Fi? Set up a private LAN connection 

For Wi-Fi, enable the chosen private LAN endpoint instead of USB.
Use **Pair another PC** to enroll that endpoint; the app stores one endpoint
and does not automatically switch between USB and LAN.
Follow the private-network guide
for routing and explicitly approved, scoped firewall configuration.

 

 

## ✨ What works today

| Capability | Available behavior |
|---|---|
| **Live desktop annotations** | Pen input produces a host overlay over the selected Windows output; the tablet mirrors it |
| **Drawing and content** | Freehand, highlighter, lines, arrows, rectangles, ellipses, circles, polygons, polylines, text and tablet clipboard images |
| **Object editing** | Single-object selection, move, rotate, resize, mirror, undo/redo and an undoable Clear |
| **Presentation tools** | Temporary laser pointer, blackboard and grid |
| **Shared navigation** | 100-400% zoom and pan on both PC and tablet, using two fingers or menu controls |
| **Pointer mode** | Stylus mouse movement, click, drag and barrel-button right-click where the pen supports it |
| **Monitor selection** | Select and switch existing PC outputs with aspect-preserving video and coordinate mapping |
| **Pairing and reconnect** | QR or manual invitation, native PC approval, certificate pinning and remembered devices |
| **Windows launcher** | Native taskbar/tray UI, explicit listener controls and a live log viewer; CLI also available |

Hold the pen still for about **550 ms**, then lift to open the radial menu.
The **Pen tools** button is an alternative. Fingers do not draw; two fingers
navigate the shared view. Read the full interaction guide.

 

## 💻 Supported devices, operating systems and connections

| Component | Current requirements and boundaries |
|---|---|
| **Windows host** | Windows 11 x64 is the primary target. The installer accepts Windows 10+, but that is not a Windows 10 validation claim |
| **Android client** | Android 11 / API 30 or later, a compatible active stylus and an H.264 decoder supporting the negotiated stream |
| **Pen** | Must be reported as a stylus by Android; hover and barrel-button capabilities depend on hardware |
| **Displays** | An existing Windows monitor or projector; no virtual monitor is created |
| **GPU** | Software encoding is available; optional NVENC requires a compatible NVIDIA GPU, driver and encoder |
| **Other platforms** | No iPadOS, macOS or Linux client/host implementation is currently provided |

Minimum OS versions are not a certified tablet list. Manufacturer-specific
stylus behavior, decoder support, DPI and fullscreen modes still need validation
on the intended setup.

| Connection | Setup |
|---|---|
| **USB / ADB** | USB data cable, tablet USB debugging and explicit PC authorization; some devices need an OEM Windows USB driver |
| **Wi-Fi / private LAN** | Tablet and PC on a trusted LAN; choose an assigned private IPv4 address on a Private/domain Windows network profile |
| **Ethernet + Wi-Fi** | The PC may be wired while the tablet uses Wi-Fi on the same LAN; this is the same TLS/TCP connection, not a separate protocol |

Control and video use **authenticated TLS/TCP**, including over USB.
No cloud account, public listener or wireless ADB is required.
Linux adapters and QUIC remain **deferred**.

 

## ⚠️ Known limitations

| Area | Important boundary |
|---|---|
| **Drawing recovery** | Update both apps for recovery support. Completed objects survive connection/app/host restarts, but restored undo/redo history, laser, selection and zoom do not. Unfinished contacts are cancelled. No export yet; uninstalling Android or clearing its app data removes saved drawings |
| **Concurrency** | One active tablet session; Android remembers one PC endpoint rather than a multi-host/transport list |
| **Desktop restrictions** | Secure desktop, UAC, protected content and exclusive fullscreen paths are not bypassed; elevated apps cannot be controlled by automatic elevation |
| **Input and editing** | Uniform stroke widths, not pressure-sensitive rendering; no eraser, per-object deletion or multi-object selection |
| **Latency and video** | Zoom pauses input until matching video is ready; capture/decoder delay varies, and translucent highlighter can briefly show extra opacity |
| **Recovery** | Video failure requires reconnecting; there is no automatic video recovery or adaptive bitrate |
| **Zoom and PC mouse** | Shared zoom does not remap the physical PC mouse; reset to 100% before using it to click desktop controls |

Release and debug APKs use different signing identities. Read the
signing and upgrade guidance
before switching; uninstalling the debug app removes its data.
Build/test success and tablet screenshots do not replace real pen,
physical-monitor, projector and fullscreen acceptance checks.

 

## 🛠️ Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Start here |
|---|---|
| USB tablet is missing or unauthorized | Check the data cable, USB debugging, tablet authorization prompt and selected device; verify with `adb devices -l` |
| Connect fails over USB | Verify that the USB listener is enabled and its ADB reverse mapping uses the same port |
| LAN connection times out | Check the chosen IP, Private/domain profile, routing, Wi-Fi client isolation and scoped firewall policy |
| Connect still uses the old USB/LAN address | Choose **Pair another PC** and pair the intended endpoint |
| Video fails or input stays suspended | Try software encoding, inspect host logs and reconnect; verify the tablet decoder supports the negotiated stream |
| Pen hold does not open tools | Hold the stylus still inside the mirrored image, or use **Pen tools**; finger holds do not open the menu |
| The host window disappears after X | It is hidden to the tray; click the tray icon or launch DrawDock again |
| Certificate pin or trust-store error | Verify the intended PC identity and file permissions; do not disable certificate validation or silently reset trust |

More detail: Android troubleshooting
and Windows video/host troubleshooting.
The Windows launcher's log viewer is the first place to inspect connection and
encoder errors. Do not publish pairing tokens, credentials or sensitive desktop captures.

 

## 🧩 Architecture

DrawDock separates **pen input**, **host-owned scene state** and **desktop video**.
The tablet sends commands; Windows renders the authoritative overlay on the
physical output, then streams that output back to the tablet.

| Component | Technology | Responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Android client | Kotlin, native Views/Canvas, MediaCodec | Stylus input, radial tools, provisional ink, H.264 decoding and pinned TLS |
| Windows host | Rust, Win32, software rasterization, FFmpeg | Click-through overlay, mouse injection, capture/encoding, pairing and listener management |
| Shared scene core | Rust `dd-scene` | Validated geometry, object transforms, canvas state and bounded undo/redo |
| Wire contract | Versioned JSON + H.264 over TLS/TCP | Separate authenticated control/video connections, source epochs and readiness barriers |

Application logic stays native; FFmpeg is an owned subprocess, not a desktop
runtime container. Learn more in Architecture,
Protocol and Video streaming.

 

## 🗺️ Roadmap

Priorities, not delivery commitments:

| Horizon | Focus |
|---|---|
| **Release readiness** | First tagged release, broader physical pen/fullscreen/projector validation and a recorded PC-plus-tablet demo |
| **Usability and performance** | More device coverage, smoother shared zoom, translucent-ink handoff and recovery under real network conditions |
| **Distribution** | Evaluate trusted Windows code signing and improve contributor/release documentation |
| **Deferred** | Linux X11/Wayland/GNOME adapters and QUIC evaluation; no support claim or implementation schedule |

Use issues to report reproducible
problems or discuss changes before expanding scope.

 

## 🤝 Contributing

Start with Development and
Architecture. Keep Rust unit tests in the existing
`tests\unit` folders and Android tests in `src\test`.
Protocol and coordinate changes usually require matching Rust and Kotlin updates.

Run the relevant checks locally after configuring the documented prerequisites:

```powershell
cargo fmt --all -- --check
cargo test --workspace
cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings
gradle -p .\android testDebugUnitTest assembleDebug lintDebug
```

GitHub Actions builds, tests and publishes **only on pushed release tags**
(`vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`), not on ordinary commits or pull requests.
See Builds and releases before tagging.

For bug reports, include OS/API versions, pen/device capabilities, transport,
encoder, reproduction steps and sanitized logs. Distinguish automated/injected
input from physical pen tests, and mark unavailable hardware checks as NOT RUN.

 

## 📚 Documentation

The **documentation index** is the entry point for the
implementation guides.

| Guide | What you will find |
|---|---|
| Development | Toolchains, source builds, tests and contribution checks |
| Windows host | Launcher, CLI, displays, listeners, logs and device administration |
| Android and ADB | Installation, USB forwarding, pairing, reconnect and troubleshooting |
| Features and interaction | Drawing tools, radial menus, transforms and presentation gestures |
| Architecture | Components, data flow, threading and lifecycle |
| Protocol | Messages, video framing, geometry epochs and resource limits |
| Pairing and threat model | Trust, credentials, permissions and security boundaries |
| Video streaming | Capture, codecs, backpressure and provisional-ink handoff |
| Brand and UI guidelines | Component-owned assets, visual tokens and interaction-preserving styling |
| Builds and releases | Tagged builds, Windows packaging, signing and third-party sources |

Implementation-aligned specifications also describe deferred design beyond the current
executable contract; use the guides above for implemented behavior.

 

## ⚖️ License

DrawDock is available under the **MIT License**.
Bundled FFmpeg/x264 components have separate **GPLv2-or-later** terms; their
notices and matching source archives accompany Windows releases.
See runtime licensing and distribution.
